speakeroldname: Mr. Denis Ethier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the most important day for forestry that this House has ever witnessed. You might even suspect that the Government had actually inspired the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) to name this as "forestry day". It provides us with a golden opportunity to record the accomplishments which the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) has achieved. He will be remembered, I assure you, as the most successful advocate of forestry that this House has ever seen.
It is my pleasant task to describe for you the cornerstone of the Government's forestry strategy, forest renewal, and then tell you how it is being implemented from coast to coast. At the outset however, I want to remind the House that the Government has pledged over $1 billion to Canadian forestry in the last two years. This is not neglect, Mr. Speaker; quite the contrary. The $1 billion represents a fundamental commitment to forest renewal, and to the wise use and conservation of Canada's most valuable natural asset, its forests.
May I begin by reminding the House that the most important issue facing the forest sector is timber supply. Local shortages of wood at a competitive cost have emerged in every Province. In the past, it was customary to harvest virgin timber and leave nature to replenish the supply. In effect, we mined the virgin forests and gave too little thought to the future crop. Forestry is now in a critical transition stage where mining must give way to systematic forest renewal and harvesting.
The limits are in sight for premium softwood sawlogs in many locations and supplies of larger, higher quality hardwood logs have been largely depleted. Pulpwood shortages are emerging in communities across the country. Only a fraction of our forests are being managed for sustained production, even today. In most cases the timber resource is renewable,

May 30, 1983
Supply
both promptly and adequately, only if action is taken immediately following harvest or natural calamity.
Even in British Columbia there are projected shortfalls. These can be prevented only by a major improvement in forest renewal performance.
The best evidence we have shows that only four Provinces have uncommitted softwood timber reserves and that these reserves are largely uneconomic because of the high costs associated with remoteness, low volume per hectare and other factors. The Provinces appear to be approximately in balance and the remaining four are in a deficit position.
Another important factor in timber supply is that averages for a large region tend to cloak severe local problems. For example, a surplus of low-quality fir pulpwood is of no value to a sawmill designed for large diameter pine and spruce logs. And a surplus of timber in one area may be too costly to move to a deficit area, even if the specifications match perfectly.
The hardwood resource contrasts sharply with the softwood situation described above. There is a marked surplus of hardwoods, with only one quarter of the allowable cut being harvested at the present time. But the hardwood expansion potential is limited almost exclusively to poplar and aspen types.
The higher value hardwood species, maple, ash, birch and walnut have been severely overcut. Canada is now importing hardwood logs, lumber and veneer for furniture and other industries. The majority of these high-value hardwoods are located on private land in the Maritimes and the southern portions of Quebec and Ontario. Even today, serious forest renewal is practically non-existent in most hardwood forests on public and private land. Interest in managing the hardwood resource is lagging at least a decade behind that for softwoods.
This description of Canada's timber supply may sound exaggerated to some, but it has been verified by recent inquiries in each of the Provinces. To others it may convey a message of pessimism and hopelessness, although this is certainly not intended.
The existing industry can be stabilized and indeed launched on a new period of expansion, provided that the challenge of forestry is understood and accepted. What is needed now is action to harness the expertise and the necessary financial resources.
Before I describe what is actually being done, allow me to remind the House of what we mean by "forest renewal". First, it is prompt regeneration, after harvest or natural losses from fire and insects. Second, it is timber stand improvements following regeneration, such as spacing, pre-commercial thinning, weeding of brush and other competing vegetation, and fertilization.
How does forest renewal fit into intensive forest management? Intensive forestry embraces all the above, and in addition includes inventory work, harvesting, protection from fire, insects and disease, planning, access roads and administration.
Forest renewal means that higher quality timber can be produced in a shorter time. It also means lower logging and handling costs to the extent that intensive treatments are applied near manufacturing plants and on less rugged terrain. The longer run gains will include higher volumes per hectare, more uniform tree size at maturity, and less decay, waste and breakage. Each of these will tend to lower costs of delivered wood and thereby contribute to our competitive capability in export markets.
The additional timber can often be made available as soon as management is accelerated. You may not have to wait until the newly planted tree matures before achieving benefits. Where an adequate volume of mature timber is still available in a timber supply area, intensive forestry gives rise to the "allowable cut effect". Simply stated, you can harvest more if you grow more. Unfortunately, the mature timber may be so badly depleted in a given area that no increase in the annual harvest is possible for two or three decades. In these cases forest renewal is geared to survival rather than expansion of the industry.
As a general rule, however, forest renewal promises substantial gains. Experience in Canada and in similar northern forests elsewhere has demonstrated that gains of 50 percent to 100 per cent or more can be achieved in volume available for harvest. Additional benefits include timber of lower cost and higher quality than can be secured through closer utilization or harvesting remote stands.
Before a decision is made to push back the forest frontier in some remote area, it would be prudent to consider first the associated public and private costs, and then compare what the equivalent expenditure would yield if directed to intensive management on lands adjacent to the mills. Today's high energy and transportation costs make it imperative that we begin to examine benefits and costs in this way.
Current expenditures on forest renewal by senior governments and industry are believed to be in the order of S300 million annually. Recent information from the Provinces indicates that an additional $100 million will have to be spent just to sustain existing harvest levels. If we are to increase the harvest in line with increasing demand for forest products and to reflect economic development opportunities, it is expected that a total annual expenditure of $650 million will be required by all parties. The foregoing estimate is based on a regular program involving increasing replanting on current cutover from 200,000 hectares to 500,000 hectares annually with genetically superior seedlings, and on increasing silvicultural treatments, such as weeding, spacing and fertilizing from
100,000	hectares to 400,000 hectares annually.
In addition, a special program area is the backlog of idle forest land. It has been mentioned as a medium-term project where federal initiative would be welcomed by Provinces and industry alike. Rehabilitation of at least 100,000 hectares annually over a decade would bring back into production a
May 30, 1983

good share of the neglected land which is adjacent to producing mills. The costs of keeping up with the current harvest and catching up with the backlog of neglected land are estimated to be S650 million annually in 1982 dollars.
Of course, better forest management will cost more. On the other side of the ledger are the expected benefits from the increment in available timber volume which, together with the anticipated increases in both real price and value added, could be expected to yield the following dividends for the Canadian economy annually: employment opportunity for 75,000 to
100,000	people in forest renewal, logging and manufacturing; increased annual sales of $22 billion, or double the present value; additional exports worth $12 billion, also double the present value; consequent benefits in related supply and service industry; increased tax revenue in excess of $1 billion.
The net revenue picture needs to be underscored. An expanding industry with a healthy resource base would generate additional tax revenue to senior governments which would be several times the additional forestry costs. In contrast, further neglect of forestry would quickly lead to widespread economic dislocation and bills of a different kind would fall due. The regional impact of the strategy would be pervasive because of the widespread importance of the sector. In the Maritimes, the first effect would be to stabilize the wood supply of the existing industry. Eventually increases in yield would allow increases in mill production. Increases in production should be possible much sooner in parts of Quebec and northern Ontario. This is particularly true of the Lakehead region where much productive forest land was not regenerated. The prairie Provinces would benefit materially from development of technology to use poplar. The greatest long-term impact, however, would probably be in British Columbia, which currently produces half of Canada's timber.
Some would argue that the federal Government has no responsibility for renewing the forest, citing provisions in the Constitution Act of 1867. Nevertheless, a historical review of federal forestry activity reveals a long-standing commitment to the forest resource and its related manufacturing sector. The pay-off has been directly in line with obvious federal responsibilities and priorities, such as: stable growth in employment; foreign exchange earnings; regional economic development; and environmental quality.
The allocation of funding responsibility varies from one Province to another. The provincial forest services have traditionally concentrated on silviculture and forest protection, with the federal Government tending to focus on silviculture by way of cost-sharing agreements and on forestry research. The private sector has concentrated on items related to timber production, such as inventory, working plans and roads, giving less attention to forest renewal and protection.
The provincial Governments now pay for the majority of forest renewal on their Crown lands, either through direct expenditures, payments to industry for work done under tenure agreements or indirect payments to industry through a stump-age offset system. Over the past ten years stumpage prices have risen dramatically. The most notable example is in Quebec, which recently announced an increase in annual
Supply
stumpage charges of 130 per cent. Other Provinces have either increased stumpage or are planning to do so. The trend is in response to a scarcity of general revenues and to the need to fund increased forest renewal programs.
The private sector's direct share in forest renewal is expected to increase sharply in this decade, judging from recent moves in several Provinces. In Newfoundland, the two major companies are now carrying nearly half the costs. They are spending $4 million annually on Crown provincial land, compared with less than half a million dollars two years ago. New Brunswick's new legislation puts a heavy demand on the large freeholder to manage land intensively. Saskatchewan is studying means to increase industry and Crown Corporation responsibility for renewal. Quebec will soon place about half the forest renewal burden on companies.
One of the principles stated in the document "Forestry Imperatives for Canada", and subscribed to by the federal Government, is that responsibility for funding maintenance of the resource should be proportionate to the benefits received. This is actually a jointly held view of the provincial and federal Governments, adopted by them within the Canadian Council of Resource Ministers.
There is another fundamental fact involved here. Federal leadership is absolutely essential to the wise use and conservation of natural resources. Forest management in Canada since 1945 has depended in large measure on joint programs. Many will recall the old Canada Forestry Act which provided complementary federal funding to the Provinces. That was before the days of DREE general development agreements and forestry subsidiary agreements. Federal leadership will be expressed once again in the new generation of forest renewal agreements, beginning with the Nova Scotia agreement in the summer of 1982. A new agreement will be implemented shortly in Prince Edward Island, and negotiations are progressing in all the other Provinces. This Government's objective is to have agreements in place in all ten Provinces by the end of this year.
In summary, there is a great deal to be done. The nature and scope of this work is fully appreciated by the federal and provincial Governments as well as by industry. Now we must find the resources to support the Canadian Forestry Service which has the lead role for the forest sector.
Forestry in Canada is indeed undergoing a transition, from exploitation of the resource to more systematic forest management. The momentum towards forest management must be increased in order to ensure that the resource is capable of sustaining current and expected levels of economic activity. Indications are that the present levels of forest renewal activity, the most important aspect of forest management, will not sustain a harvest level sufficient to fulfil future needs.
Finally, the climate for co-operation has never been better across the country. I hope and expect that all the Parties in this House will join with the Government in the cause of forest renewal.

Madam Speaker, we cannot afford to degrade our vital land resources because there exists a fundamental interdependence between energy and land resources in the world and Canada. As our farm land is continually shrinking, the need for conservation of this scarce resource becomes more and more pressing. Only 13 per cent of our total land area can support agricultural activity, yet substantial crop land is lost annually by soil erosion. The continual degradation of land requires increased quantities of fossil energy in the form of fertilizers and other inputs to offset lost soil productivity.
According to calculations by U.S. specialists in soil erosion, an estimated five-gallon equivalent of fuel per acre is used to offset the soil erosion loss on crop land. On the estimated 281 million acres in production in Canada, 1.4 billion gallons of fuel equivalents have to be used annually to offset past losses. This equals some 40 million barrels of oil annually, or about 30 per cent of our oil imports. The direct cost of erosion to the prairie farm economy is estimated at $368 million a year. The total soil loss due to erosion equals a yearly yield reduction of more than 71,000 tonnes of wheat. These high figures point out how acute the problem of soil erosion is and its implications in terms of future high energy inputs and lost potential.

Madam Speaker, Bill C-155 has inflamed separatism in Alberta. Hundreds of loyal Albertans are now asking: will Alberta ever get a fair deal from Ottawa?
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) astonished and pleased Albertans when he indicated that he would follow the Gilson recommendations and pay the shortfall of the Crow to the producers. In every part of the Province hope was rekindled. Finally, Alberta hog and cattle producers and processors were going to be able to build their industry and find new markets. But the glad tidings were shortlived. The same Minister, ashamed even to face the House, announced across the street from the Parliament Buildings that the Government had changed his mind, that the shortfall would not be paid to the producers after all but to the railways, thus sentencing Albertans once more to be "drawers of water", for the benefit of Quebec.
It is rumoured that the Minister wanted to give the West a chance but that the Quebec Liberal Caucus and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), helped by Ministers from Quebec, forced him to change his mind. If this is so, the Hon. Minister should resign rather than remain the chattel of one Province. This action told western Canada and the world that the interests of Quebec come first, and the rest of Canada can have the crumbs. Mr. Trudeau is not heading the Government of Canada, he is the head of a Government of and for Quebec. If this Liberal Government is hell bent on breaking up Canada, it is surely going about it in the right way. 1 give fair warning: Albertans are not going to accept this kind of treatment very much longer.

Madam Speaker, the Liberal Government does not seem satisfied enough with having many fishermen in Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, and New Brunswick out of work; now it is carrying the fight into the Magdalen Islands.
The fight between the Quebec and Canadian Governments over the licensing of six fishing vessels owned by Madelipeche Incorporated is wreaking havoc on the livelihood of 500 families on the Magdalen Islands. The Minister stated in the House last week that his primary concern is to prevent a precedent being set. While this may have some merit further down the line, the immediate problem is to get those fishermen and shoreworkers back on the job. They have already lost a third of their fishing season. In a region which is under severe economic hardship, such a loss is devastating.
The Minister and his Quebec counterpart can continue their long term negotiations, but it is imperative that they first enter into an interim agreement which would allow fishing to resume and the plant to reopen. This dispute is between the two Governments, and it should be dealt with in Government offices, not on the backs of the fishermen and their communities.

SIZE OF DEFICIT-ENUMERATION OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Finance Minister (Mr. Lalonde) have the unmitigated gall to criticize our ally, the United States, for its high deficit and interest rates as causing our economic woes, when our own deficit is at record levels and is nothing but a deferred tax being foisted on our children.

May 30, 1983

Our deficit must come down. speechtext: Madam Speaker, Canadian policy and Canadian law with respect to exports of military equipment are well known. An export permit is required for each export shipment. After the New York Times printed an article about the possibility that Canadian bullets were being used in Nicaragua, we made enquiries within the Department that issues export permits. The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Oberle:
That this House condemns the Government for its neglect of Canada's forests and its indifference to the threat posed to Canada's forests and forest industries by pests, fire, pollution and foreign competition, and calls upon the Government to stimulate the research needed to promote superior growth and diversify export products, and acknowledge its responsibility to protect the Canadian environment and the millions of Canadians whose livelihood depends upon Canada's forest resources.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest that we owe a debt to the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) for having provided this opportunity to raise a matter of prime importance to Canada. I should like to put the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) at his ease a little bit because he was worried about the language used in the motion. As far as I am concerned the wording stands. It begins as follows:
That this House condemns the Government for its neglect of Canada's forests and its indifference to the threat posed-
I should like to inform the Minister here and now that as far as I am concerned the purpose of the debate is to strengthen his hand with his Cabinet colleagues so that we will no longer have to condemn the Government for its neglect of our forest lands.
From time immemorial our forests have been relentlessly attacked by fire caused by lightning and by pests. Happily the destructive efforts of these two plagues are intermittent and forests have somehow or other managed to survive. Now a
May 30, 1983

third attack on the forests has been launched and is being sustained. The forests are beginning to show excessive wear and tear. Many a qualified forester indeed will tell you that our forests are being used up under this new threat.
Whence does this threat come? From man, with his insatiable hunger for wood products either to protect him from the elements, the wind and the cold, or when that does not work, products on which he can blow his nose when he has a cold or to record his thoughts-some good thoughts and some not so good. Modern man could be the forest's greatest foe; if man wants the forest to help him he will have to co-operate with the forest and not be content with destroying it.
Yet modern man has within him the power, if properly awakened and awakened soon enough, to repair the damage he has done and preserve that valuable heritage for generations to come. A warning was given to us in Canada over a century ago; we have yet to show that we have heeded that caution. John A. Macdonald said in 1871 and I quote:
We are recklessly destroying the timber of Canada. There is scarcely a possibility of replacing it. It occurs to me that the subject should be looked in the face and some efforts made for the preservation of our timber.
What prompted this comment, it would seem, was the sight of the destruction of the white pine in Ontario. Records indicate that in the winter of 1866 and 1867, 400 men felled nearly 30,000 huge white pines. In less than a century the white pine forests that once covered large parts of eastern Canada has been reduced almost to a memory. There remain only a few lonely giants which were skipped by the cutting crews.
Speaking of lonely giants, and I hope they are not too lonely, I should like to tell the House that in British Columbia MacMillan Bloedel provided a sanctuary by preserving a small park where there is a majestic stand of Douglas fir and cedar which is called Cathedral Grove. It straddles the road crossing Vancouver Island west of Parksville on the way to the Pacific Rim Park. It has to be seen to be believed. There, in Cathedral Grove-how aptly named!-one strains backward and upward to see them rise, 250 to 300 feet tall, 30 and 40 feet in girth. Those trees were standing tall-20 feet or so-when King John-John Lackland-in 1215 was forced on to Runnymede Island to sign the Magna Carta, 700 years ago. That is what the forest can do.
Our resolve to preserve our forests may need stimulation. Let us consider this debate as a stimulant; let it be a catalyst; let it be anything you like provided it provokes positive reaction and promotes sustained activity in favour of forest regeneration. I repeat to the Minister, we are here to strengthen his hand with Cabinet.
Let us remember above all else that we have it in our hands-and we are at a crossroads as many a forester will tell you-to do one of two things. We can ensure that our consumption of the forests will not devastate the forests, or we can say to the generations which come after us: "Tough; we used your forests, but it never occurred to us to put them back, to regenerate them for your use".
Supply
Are we prepared to act today to earn the gratitude of our grandchildren or will they curse us for our wanton wastefulness? The motto of my first alma mater, Mr. Speaker, was "Tuum est", "It's up to you". I believe our motto should be "Nostrum est", "It's up to us". It is up to us. We can go either way. We can preserve and deserve thanks, or we can destroy and merit obloquy.
How important is conservation? Aside altogether from the value of the timber cut, there is the value of the timber standing. Trees-and mark this, Mr. Speaker-or their absence, produce our climate. Rain forests or deserts? These are the outside options. Within those outer brackets, Mr. Speaker, we have the option of renewing forests and grasslands or facing a future of desert. Which do we want?
This debate today, for me at least, is an exercise aimed at reaching out for and activating the springs of action of the public, in both levels of Government and in industry. It is an exhortation to action. For that reason, I personally am extremely grateful to the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle). That is the best we can do on this side of the House. However, I would like to remind all listening that even during those brief nine or ten months in office the Progressive Conservative Government took major steps to restore the federal forestry service to its rightful place by appointing a knowledgeable and enthusiastic forester as the Assistant Deputy Minister of Forestry, a man who knows how to get his message across to Ministers and to the public. We are grateful to him and I am happy to acknowledge his presence under our roof today.
Much more needs to be done, much, much more. Somehow or other we have to provoke, inspire, encourage, lobby, incite, instigate, and perhaps even coax a little or wheedle. The Greeks had a word for it which we borrowed, "ecphorize", meaning to remove obstacles. That is what we must do, Mr. Speaker; we must remove obstacles, whether they be caused by ignorance, lethargy or red tape.
How do we do that? I think perhaps the shock treatment might help and I would like to deliver a few shocks. I believe they are shocks. They were shocks to me when I first became aware of them. For example, let us consider the revenue which this country receives from all quarters and the revenue it receives from forestry, its expenditures across the country and its expenditures on forestry. It is really quite interesting when you realize that the revenue from the forests, grosso modo, is about 1 per cent of the revenue expected by this Government this year, and its expenditures on forestry are about .1 per cent. That is a shameful comparison; I hope it shocks you, Mr. Speaker. One per cent in terms of revenue to the federal Government and 0.1 per cent in expenditures on forestry.
The Food and Agriculture Organization reported recently that the forest land base of the world is disappearing at the rate of 50 acres a minute. This is around the world; it is not just a Canadian problem, Mr. Speaker, I admit that. However, we do not have to lag behind. It is the livelihood of a good many Canadians. It is the basis of our foreign trade. The forest

Supply
land of the world is disappearing at the rate of 50 acres a minute. If you worked that out in other terms, it is about 72,000 acres a day, about 112 square miles a day, of 41,000 square miles a year, almost the size of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick combined. That amount of forest land is disappearing from the face of the earth every year.
Something else which I believe is a real shocker is that to produce one day's issue of the Toronto Sun requires seven acres of bush to be chopped down, 2,400 acres per year. That is four square miles per year for one paper. And that is just one paper in one metropolican city in Canada. What about the New York Times'? How many acres or square miles are required even for the Sunday edition of the New York Times?
One thing we seem to forget, Mr. Speaker, and that is that trees take a long time to grow, but if permitted they will grow and stand tall. Once they are chopped down, however, or burned out, or eaten by pests, they take years to replace. The present Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts)-I am happy to see he is still in the House-was quoted in something 1 read recently as saying: "There will be a disaster in our forest heritage if we let nature take its course". He was speaking of forest fires and infestations. 1 say that there will be an even greater disaster if we let man have his way without inducing him one way or another to replant whatever he fells.
Let us look at what we stand to lose if we lose our forest industry. The total production value from our forests is about $13 billion, of which approximately $9 billion is for export. Total public revenues from forests to both levels of Government, federal and provincial, are about $2 billion. Forest products account for about 18 per cent, nearly one-fifth of Canada's total exports. Forest products are far and away the most important of Canada's exports. It has already been mentioned but it is worth underlining, Mr. Speaker, that forestry makes a larger, positive contribution to our trade balance than agriculture, fisheries, mining and petroleum products combined. Forestry produces more than those four industries. Forestry directly or indirectly employs one out of every ten Canadians in the work force. That is a very important consideration.
What are we doing partially that we ought to be doing more thoroughly? At what sort of rate are we reforesting or restoring to the ground that which we are taking from it? Sweden, about the size of Alberta, plants 400 million seedlings a year. That country is just about one-tenth the size of Canada south of the 60th parallel. Who plants these seedlings? It is the industry which plants them. Canada plants from coast to coast about 350 million seedlings. We ought to be planting three times as many trees, Mr. Speaker. Even then we would still not be up to the rate at which Sweden plants trees. We plant only one acre for every four acres harvested, and nature provides another acre. So we have two unplanted and infertile. That is a disgraceful record and we need to and could do more, not for ourselves but for those who follow us.

Let us look at some of the more disconcerting facts. The federal Government receives about $1 billion annually from
forest enterprises and the federal forestry budget amounts to about $66 million, or roughly 6.5 per cent of the revenue that forestry generates. The other figures I have already mentioned. Provincial Governments derive about the same amount but they do not do all that much better. Over all, no more than 20 per cent of the revenue from the forest is restored to the forest. Only $400 million across this whole country for an industry which produces $12 billion to $13 billion in products and $9 billion in export earnings.
This is an age of buzzwords, I suppose, Mr. Speaker, and the buzzwords I would like to get out and about on everyone's tongue are "forest management", and "sustainable yield". Those are the important objectives which have to be formulated and pursued consistently year after year after year. A 20, 30 or 40 year program has to be laid down. We have to farm our forests properly, and I use the word "farm" advisedly. We have to plant seeds as a farmer plants seeds if we want a crop down the road. I have heard, for example, that there have been notions of putting seeds in little pellets and spreading them out from an aircraft flying over cut land. Not all will germinate, but many of them will and take root.
We also have to thin the forests to make sure that the hardiest trees survive and produce the best crop. We have to plant today at a rate which will give us the crop we are going to need 20 or 30 years hence. We have to cull and thin and in places even fertilize. I understand the Swedes fertilize their trees, which is an interesting concept and it can be done. It will take a lot of tender loving care as well as scientific knowledge.
In the care of our forests today, we are behaving not much better than our forefathers who managed to demolish the white pine so effectively in such a short time, as Sir John A. reminded us over 100 years ago.

Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed very much the presentation of the Hon. Member. He pointed out many important issues. However, there is one glaring omission and I wonder if he might take a moment to comment. It might have simply been an inadvertent oversight.
In Canada, especially in the particular areas represented by the Hon. Member and myself, there are thousands and thousands of native people. The economy of most of their communities is based on Unemployment Insurance and welfare. They do not have access to the forest industry. Does the Hon. Member care to make a statement as to why native people were omitted from the resolution and why there has been no assistance from the federal Government so that the native people can gain access to the forest resource and its development? The native land claims are the key by which they could be given access to this resource and thereby strengthen the economy of the native communities. The land claim is one of the few mechanisms by which native people can have access to forest resources in a fair and equitable way.
The Hon. Member mentioned that the biggest engine of the Canadian economy was the forest industry, so why has his Party neglected to place in its resolution before the House of
May 30, 1983

Commons a statement on the access by native people to that forest resource?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) for drawing to my attention that omission. Twenty minutes was all I was permitted. I had hoped that I would be able to include something along those lines because it has to be remembered that the federal Government, which has a tendency to say it is all the Provinces' fault, that they should do more for forestry because they own the resource, itself tends to forget there is an area of Canada south of 60 and about the size of Nova Scotia which is federal Crown land. Much of that land is taken up by reserves where the Indians would be happy to develop a forest industry to supply existing mills or to build mills of their own. They could earn their living in that way. That was mentioned in many of the things I read to prepare myself for this debate today, but the 20-minute rule prevented me from developing it any further. I do hope the Hon. Member will do so.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in this debate. I am very pleased at the very constructive position taken both by the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) and the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). I agree with all of the comments that the latter Member has made, except for his assumption that the Government was not sympathetic to the representations being made by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) who is responsible for the Canadian Forestry Service.
speakername: Hon.   J.-J. Blais@Minister of Supply and Services

speechtext: Not sufficiently sympathetic.

In fact, there has been a great deal of support given to the Minister concerning the forestry policies he has advanced. Indeed, I am sure the hon. gentleman will recognize there has been more activity in the forest sector in the last three years than at any time before by the federal Government. The Government has assumed a leadership role at the national level which in my view, it ought to have assumed some time before. But in view of that assumption by the Minister of the Environment, I think we ought to commend him for having taken that initiative.
I can well recognize why the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River would be in love with the forest. I had occasion last summer to take my family into the interior of British Columbia and I insisted on travelling two days on lumber roads up and down the mountainside to observe the size of the forest.
How is your car?

The car is fine. It was a rented car. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that that forest is as bountiful, attractive and beautiful as anyone would want. I ahve a particular love for the forest because I come from northern Ontario. It just so happens that this year is the one hundredth anniversary of my great grandfather's arrival in northern Ontario where he
Supply
worked for E.B. Eddy at the time they were cutting ties for the CPR which was then starting its long journey across the country to the region represented by my hon. friend. I can tell him that since that time my family, which has now become bountiful and plentiful also, occupies a large number of areas in northern Ontario and a large number of my family are involved in the forest products industry. So I felt very emotional having observed that which the hon. gentleman speaks of.
As well I was very sensitive to his comments relating to the white pine, the prince of pines, and its demise from northern Ontario forests. That is a calamity and a tragedy which we will hopefully be able to reverse.
It must not happen again.

Not only must it not happen again, there must be a greater aggressivity on the part of the Ontario Government, a Province where these trees are found, to develop nurseries and grow seeds that will permit the replenishment of the forests in northern Ontario, not only with jack pine, red pine and spruce but also with white pine. It takes over 100 years for that tree to grow to full maturity. It requires a longsighted Government to recognize that, notwithstanding the fact it may take 125 years for the tree to grow to full maturity in northern Ontario, there is a responsibility to future generations of Canadians to plant and nurture now.
I agree with the hon. gentleman that we must begin to farm that resource now, which is an essential ingredient in my view.
It has been the history of humankind to exploit forests and to denude the land of forests. That was the phenomenon in the Middle East. We can base ourselves on the Holy Scriptures, both the Old Testament and the New Testament, where we see that there were forests there. They were not plentiful but they did exist. The fact is that in North Africa those forests are now gone, an area which I had the pleasure of visiting. In biblical times the atlas cedar grew there in bountiful quantities. It has now disappeared. It has disappeared to the point where it has become nearly a sacred material in the Moslem religion and is being incorporated in all their rites. The reason is that wood is as close to humanity as any material can be. It was the first hard material capable of being utilized by our ancestors. The fact is that it is being utilized now to an even greater extent than it was in those days.
Coming from northern Ontario I am even more sensitive to its importance. In terms of economic impact, the forest industry in northern Ontario is responsible for 55 per cent of all manufacturing jobs. That represents 31,000 jobs. It is responsible for 58 per cent of manufacturing wages and salaries, or some $560 million on an annual basis. It is reponsible for 57 per cent of the value of production, namely $2.2 billion. It is responsible for 54 per cent of value added to products in northern Ontario.
It is evident from each of the statistics that I have quoted that more than half the economic activity in northern Ontario

Supply
is attributable to the forest products industry. But the state of Ontario's forests is not very good. I can speak of my own riding where I said, in a speech I made on the forest products industry seven years ago, that we had but 15 years left of marketable timber in the region. Very little has been done since then. In the Province of Ontario, 3.8 million hectares are depleted at this stage. The total number of acres needing reforestation would translate into 37,650 square kilometres. That is 37,650 square kilometres of backlog in northern Ontario which needs to be reseeded and put back into production.
Ontario's annual cut is 160,000 hectares, but its reforestation is in only half that area, that is, 80,000 hectares. Even with the huge backlog of over 37,000 square kilometres of forests which need to be replenished, it is falling behind 50 per cent annually. In Ontario twice as much is being cut as is being planted, and that is completely unacceptable.
In fact, the Province of Ontario has long been very weak in forest management. This is understandable when all the decisions relating to the forest products industry are being made in hogtown. I have nothing against Toronto, the Queen City, but the fact is that it is far removed from those areas where lumber is being exploited.
As I indicated, my family has been in northern Ontario for 100 years. We have attempted on a number of occasions to improve and encourage the improvement of forest management, but to no avail. The operators in northern Ontario are very much aware of the need for reseeding. Unfortunately, the private operators must meet the market and its requirements. Their profit margins are very slight and one cannot expect an operator, who tends to operate in terms of the benefits which will flow into his own treasury at the end of any given fiscal year of operation, to look 125 years down the line. We cannot expect him to finance the operation 125 years into the future or even 50 years down the line. It is only a public authority which really ought to have that kind of foresight. In the past the Ontario Government has shown a desire for the private sector to fund forest management and renewal. Of course, that did not happen.
The private sector is interested in immediate exploitation and is not looking forward to forest conservation in the long term. That is where the failure is. Finally, after stimulation by the federal Government, the Province of Ontario has agreed to enter into forest management agreements with the producers in the Province of Ontario. It has signed agreements with 13 producers in order to provide them with funding that would match or take into account the contribution from the private sector in order to enter into forest management agreements. While that is not representative of all the suppliers. It is better than nothing.
In effect, that agreement which was signed by the Government of Ontario and the Government of Canada provided for $82 million in investments over five years. That agreement will terminate in March, 1984, and the renegotiation of a new agreement is being undertaken. That new agreement will envision intensive efforts to reforest private and industrial lands as well as provide for the regeneration of the backlog of
unsatisfactorily restocked Crown land. It will also provide for the expansion of nursery capacity since that capacity is insufficient. It is nearly one-third of what should be available. Furthermore, it proposes increased research and development in Ontario to meet that Province's specific requirements. It also takes into account Indian reserves forest management. The hon. gentleman from the New Democratic Party spoke about Indian lands and the fact that forests are the only resource available for exploitation by Indian people in a large number of those areas. Exactly the same situation exists in my area. One band has close to 50,000 acres of available forests for exploitation but has never before been encouraged to exploit that resource. I have obtained funds for them so they may exploit those resources in the future.
In addition, we will have technology transfers and increased public awareness, which is essential. This brings me to the subject of forest fires and the threat of forest fires which, in 1980, were responsible for the destruction of an equivalent of a six kilometre wide strip of forest from coast to coast in Canada and a $350 million loss in terms of income. As a result of that particular loss in 1980, I have been aggressively seeking to obtain the sort of firefighting equipment which is required for the firefighting patrol Canada.
That is why I went after the CL-2I5, a water bomber manufactured by Canadair. It is the most effective instrument we have, and it makes it easier to put out a fire when it first starts, as a result of lightning or electric storms in areas that are not accessible by road. The only way to get there is by air, and in that kind of situation, the best kind of aircraft is a plane, and the CL-215 was designed especially for fighting forest fires. This plane, which is entirely Canadian-designed, can carry more than seven tons of water per trip and make ten trips per hour.

That means seven tonnes per trip, ten trips per hour, 70 tonnes of water which can be dumped on to a fire anywhere water can be scooped. All that is required for the scooping is 1,200 metres, which is just a bit more than one kilometre. It can come in, scoop the water and take off with seven tonnes of water.
We have been able to export the aircraft. We have 15 of those aircraft flying in France, 17 flying in Spain, 12 flying in Greece, four in Yugoslavia, two in Venezuela, two in Thailand and two in Italy. In effect, with the orders that we are placing jointly with the Provinces, we will be in a position to encourage greater aggressivity by Canadair in the international marketplace. It is an aicraft which is required. It is an aircraft which not only provides us with protection against fires in the forest, but also one which provides a large number of jobs in a very sensitive area of Canadian industrial activity, namely, the aerospace industry.

It is an industry which will secure for us not only domestic markets, but also export markets for long periods of time, if we are wise enough to farm the resource, if we are wise enough to put back as much into forest management as we take out of it. It is something which we have not done in the past. We have been able to survive because Canada was so plentiful.

Booth going up the Ottawa River, the Mattawa River and then finding all the best white pines, topping the white pines, taking the best 16 feet and leaving the balance in the bush. One of its Members must be speaking next. I hope that they will be as constructive in their approach as were the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) and the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro).
In concluding, I want to transmit some praise to my colleague and seatmate, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), because he has dealt with all the areas which have been identified in the motion. If one considers the motion, one finds that it condemns the Government for neglect but identifies the areas, all of which have been addressed by the Minister. Indeed, the pest problem has been well addressed by the Canadian Forestry Service. There is still work to be done. I have already discussed fire control and the amount of moneys we are investing in the water bomber. In terms of pollution, again there is work concerning acid rain. In terms of foreign competition as well, I have discussed our ability to penetrate the American market and to resist the protectionist measures which the Americans threatened to take.

I would like to make one last point. Last January, all the caucus Members from northern Ontario met in Thunder Bay and we dealt with forest products and the forest industry. We invited all Hon. Members from northern Ontario, including one Hon. Member from the Loyal Opposition. There were six Cabinet Ministers, all of whom had an interest, direct or indirect, in the forest products industry. We invited members of the private sector who were involved in pulp and paper, in sawmill operations, in planing and drying operations, in order to discuss the industry and the measures which should be taken by the Government in order to advance the industry's cause. The results of that particular conference are now being implemented in large measure. One of them has been implemented because there was a recommendation by the industry relating to water bombers, and that has gone forward. However, the others are now being worked upon and are being implemented by the Canadian Forestry Service.
I think that the Government has done a great deal. There is still a great deal to be done, but what it has done, primarily, has been to assume the leadership role in the protection and in the exploitation of our forests, which really devolves upon the Government of Canada.
