Mr. Speaker, listening to the Hon. Member and his constructive remarks in response to the motion which is filed under my name, one cannot help but be reminded of the old saying that if he could only harness the energy expended in talking of the crisis, it would very soon be ended. There is no question but that the Liberals have done much talking and, hopefully, sooner or later, their talking will be followed up with some action.
The Minister made reference to a very important subject, one very dear to my heart, that is, the development of private woodlots and the necessity for developing government programs and regimes which would encourage and entice private owners of marginal farmland which should be forested or private owners of woodlands to begin planting and restocking. As he said, it would take 25 years to 100 years, so there is really no great incentive for anyone, in one life time, to undertake such a project. He heaped scorn on the Province for not being more innovative in encouraging people. Could he tell me what initiatives are being taken by the federal Government? The Tax Act really comes under federal Government jurisdiction. What initiative is the federal Government taking to develop a tax regime which would encourage and entice private woodlot owners, industries and Provinces to follow suit and match the efforts of the federal Government in that kind of endeavour?

Mr. Speaker, the development of woodlots, of course, would have to come within the agreements which are executed and would have to be envisaged within the agreements which are being negotiated as between the federal Government and the provincial Government.

May 30, 1983
Supply
I am not one to start encouraging the federal Government to engage in a confrontational stance vis-a-vis the Provinces in an area as important as the forest products industry. I would fear that if the Government of Canada would unilaterally start offering incentives to private entrepreneurs in terms of the development of private woodlots, especially where Provinces have huge areas of forestry which come under provincial Crown jurisdiction, we would get into that sort of confrontational stance. Elowever, I recognize that in certain areas that may be the only way to go. I know that in the Province of Quebec the question of the development of private woodlots and the incentives being advanced by the federal Government in terms of the development of private woodlots is one of the options at which the Government is looking.
In my area the Province controls most of the Crown lands, except for Indian lands in certain areas. Therefore, it tends to be able to adopt its own policies in order to favour the Crown lands within the Province, and private woodlot operators tend to benefit as a result of the spin-offs of provincial policy. Having said that, the best way to address the individual situations in individual Provinces is to negotiate terms affecting private woodlots within federal-provincial agreements.

Mr. Speaker, the answer of the previous speaker reminds me of the old saying that talk is cheap but it takes money to make things move. I wonder where his priority was in the 20 minutes he took. Would the Minister be prepared to indicate what kind of support he would give to native people across Canada for access into the forest industry? I would just like to mention two or three things. One would be access to the resource. There is a desperate need to resolve the land claim issue and to give them access. Does he support that? The second is the creation of a native forest development corporation for the funding and for the development of silviculture inventory, reseeding and production. The third would be the establishment of an Indian forest economic development fund, a special fund so that native people can become involved in it. The fourth would be an affirmative action program where in companies are financially assisted by the federal Government, whether they be Crown Zellerbach or MacMillan Bloedel. Would the Government be prepared to undertake an affirmative action program so that young Indian people will have employment opportunities in forestry operations? The fifth would be the development of specific training programs for young people so that they can become directly involved in that industry. The sixth would be some form of co-operation between the Department of the Environment and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to develop an effective forestry program for native people. Would the Minister raise these with his caucus colleagues and press for them as a member of the Cabinet of this Government?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) who went on at
some length in his speech describing the excellent deal in terms of fire-fighting aircraft on which the federal Government has taken initiative. I want to say that I agree with him in part, that in fact it was an important breakthrough and will assist many Provinces. However, the Province with the major component in the Canadian forest industry is the Province of British Columbia and its neighbouring territory, Yukon. The aircraft which the federal Government is now pushing takes considerable time to land, to pick up water and to take off once again. When the Government made the decision, did it overlook the fact that British Columbia does not have wide valleys and easy access to water sources? More specifically, did the Government consider that a good deal of northern British Columbia and Yukon are fighting forest fires when all the lakes are frozen over, particularly at this time of the year and still for many, many weeks? How could the Government see using this aircraft to scoop up water to fight forest fires when the lakes are frozen over?

First, the Hon. Member says that it takes a long time for the aircraft to land in order to load on water. The fact is that the aircraft does not land. It takes six seconds to scoop up water. It needs only a bit more than a kilometre to go from 50 feet above land or water, to dip down and load something over seven tonnes of water, and then to take off again.
Did you say 50 feet?
Yes, just slightly over one kilometre or 1,200 metres is what is required for the aircraft to dive from 50 feet above ground level-
In British Columbia they wou have to be higher than 50 feet.

The fact is that the aircraft can do it. I have asked that specific question of my officials who told me that in British Columbia the aircraft would be very useful, even more useful than the fire retardant bombers that are now being employed there.
However, the situation in British Columbia is that there are a number of companies using older type aircraft such as the DC-6 and some smaller type of aircraft which are using fire retardants. I think there may be some pressure by those contractors vis-a-vis the British Columbia Government relating to their getting involved with water bombers.
In terms of the Yukon Territory, I can tell the Hon. Member that indeed in my area of the country where lakes are frozen over for some period of time, when there is ice on the lakes, there is snow in the bush and when there is snow in the bush, there is very little chance of fire starting. In fact, that is the case in Yukon as well. The survey at which we looked indicated that while there are some forest fires in the early portions of the season, the high incident of forest fires is after the lakes are opened and there can be the scooping of water and dumping of water on to fires.
In addition, we have looked at lakes and the availability of lakes close to where valuable forest lands are to be found. We
May 30, 1983

have ascertained that the lakes are sufficiently close to make the water bomber a viable firefighting mechanism.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of Hon. Members who have participated so far, particularly to those of the Hon. Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais). My family, like his, has had a bit of a feel for the forests. We were chased out of Scotland a bit earlier than his family arrived in this country because the English at that time preferred sheep, and we landed in Nova Scotia. Ever since that time my family has been interested in forestry. My own grandfather began to plant trees over 60 years ago. My father has continued this tradition, and so have I. It makes me laugh when I hear the Minister say that it is only the public sector which has a commitment to undertake long-term forestry projects. It has to be a partnership between the public and the private sector. When I think of the shortsighted policies that have existed in the public sector with respect to forestry and compare them with some of the things that industrialists like K. C. Irving have done to entertain large scale forestry, I realize just how out of touch the Minister is.
At one time Canada had a federal forestry department. Its first Minister was a distinguished former Premier of New Brunswick, Hugh John Flemming. He was also an outstanding Member of the House for many years. However, at this point in time the forestry department has been merged or submerged into the greater Department of the Environment. This is not acceptable because the size of the contribution of this Department would dictate that it certainly deserves equal status to agriculture and to fisheries. It is pretty obvious that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan)-to whom I want to pay tribute for doing something which our administration suggested should be done and which we had begun to do, that is, to move the PFRA back into that Department where it should have been and extend services across the country- would be the first to agree that forestry deserves equal status to agriculture. I am sure the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) would agree as well. It is unfortunate that this step cannot be taken.
As other Hon. Members have said-and I think it should be put on the record once more-the forestry sector deserves at least equal treatment because directly or indirectly it provides one out of every ten jobs in the country. It provides jobs for 13 per cent of all people employed in manufacturing and generates over $1 billion in tax revenue for the Provinces. Forest products exports, as the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) said, amount to many billions of dollars and account for about 18 per cent of all Canadian exports. It makes a larger positive net contribution to trade, as he said, than agriculture, mining, fisheries and the petroleum industry combined, yet the forest industry has been downgraded over the years simply because it has not been making the demands or has not received the attention that it should have.
Supply
People tend to view forests in extremes. Some, like the American poet Joyce Kilmer who was killed during World War I, were very eloquent on the subject. Who can forget his testimony that "Poems are made by fools like me, but only God can make a tree".
On the other hand there are those pragmatic individuals who run large pulp companies or who take part in some other sectors of the industry who look upon forests as only the raw material for cellulose or as a source for so many cunits of lumber. I believe that this important industry has to be viewed with enlightened concern, a blending if you will of the aesthetic and the practical so that this great renewable resource is administered and developed, if not with idealism, at least with sensitivity for all that it can do and what it represents and has represented for this country.
The federal Government has been slowly responding to problems in the forestry sector caused by past neglect. Evidence of this growing federal concern has been indicated as speakers on the Government side have emphasized, by the initiation of a shared-cost program for modernization of the forest products industry. Major increases in federal input to forest management through DREE sub-agreements with the Provinces has been another initiative which has been helpful. There was the decision to raise the Canadian Forestry Service to a separate service headed by an Assistant Deputy Minister and the establishment of the federal forestry sector strategy committee to co-ordinate and assess federal initiatives and actions relation to the forestry sector. More effort is needed. Certainly there has to be a greater effort made by the provincial as well as the federal Governments if we are going to continue to stop the neglect and the discrimination of this great industry.
Some people may say we do not need a federal forest Minister because so much of the jurisdiction lies with the Provinces. That is not so. Even excluding the vast Territories, Yukon and N.W.T. in this country, there are still areas of land under the control of the federal Government in Provinces that are greater in total area than the Province of Nova Scotia.
It seems obvious that to deny a resource of this magnitude a separate Ministry is a situation that should not be allowed to continue. The different regions of Canada have their own traditions. It is fascinating how the history of forestry blends in with the history of this country. Each region has its own methodology, from the rain forests of British Columbia to the Acadian forests in eastern Canada. There have been different historical developments and different ways of life which have developed.
In our school it was interesting to learn how the lumberjacks in New Brunswick and Maine almost caused a war between our two countries, called "The Pork and Beans War", when they began to take umbrage at certain things that went on in the forests in their Province and State respectively.
Our national capital was once a lumber town. That was the very reason for its existence at the time that Queen Victoria

May 30, 1983
Supply
decided it had the potential to be the capital of Canada. Some cynics would agree that it made a greater contribution as a timber centre than it has ever made as a political centre. That probably is a topic for another speech.
As a Member of Parliament from Nova Scotia, I am proud to say there was no Province in the country that had a more unique approach to the ownership of land and the utilization of forests. It has been a remarkably cosmopolitan Province in terms of the evolution of this country's history. To deviate from the strict topic of forestry for a moment, let me say that upon its stage many dramas involving Britain, France and the United States were once played. It was a gateway for French exploration. It was a British military staging ground and became, as the great author Thomas H. Riddell stated when talking about the Port of Halifax, "The warden of the north" which stood guard over the vast interior of this country for many years. Our Province was front and centre during the fraternal struggle between Great Britain and the United States.
From the War of Independence to the United States' Civil War, Irish, Scots, Germans and United Empire loyalists, people from Quebec or France, all for their own good reasons, settled in Nova Scotia, and a unique land system evolved. The ownership of land always meant a great deal to the people of Nova Scotia, and no other Province in the country, to my knowledge, had such a high percentage of private land ownership, free from encumbrances.
Nova Scotia achieved great prosperity from the so-called square timber trade and the use of its high-grade of spruce and pine, not only for shipbuilding and the supplying of masts for the British Navy, but also because Napoleon's blockades in Europe dictated that new sources of timber be found. The result was that the beams and interiors of many large and stately structures, residences and public buildings in Great Britain have come from the forests of Nova Scotia. However, as the Minister of Supply and Services pointed out, in his region this high grading of resources took a very high toll. It was very bad for the general health of our forests. After this industry reached its peak in the late 1800s replanting and other steps to repair the quality and the extent of our forests have never to this day been adequately undertaken.
Also, there has been a dramatic change from a sawlog to a pulpwood type of economy. It has been only in the last 25 years that any significant amount of reforestation has been undertaken. I want to again pay tribute to K. C. Irving for what he has done in the Province of New Brunswick and to mention that some of the large forest companies in Nova Scotia have come to a belated realization that they have to put something back in, that they have to take part in reforestation and make certain that the kinds of trees that are planted are of good quality.
At the present time there has to be, as other speakers have said, a great deal of work undertaken to improve the forestry sector. I want to speak primarily about eastern Canada. Various diseases affecting both hard and soft woods have
caused great losses to Nova Scotia. Our beech, birch and now our elm have been affected. Logging practices in recent years have been abominable. Heavy equipment has been taken in and the land has been scarred. New growth has been destroyed, which has led to erosion and very severe damage to the environment. Small streams are clogged with brush and silt. The situation has become very offensive to people who care about forestry and the environment.
I believe that one of the things that both the Nova Scotia Government and the federal Government can do is to encourage the retention and expansion by private land owners of the small woodlot holdings they have. This, as I mentioned earlier, is part of the historical pattern that characterized our Province. Much can be done to encourage such ownership. Better forest management and marketing opportunities for small land owners can be facilitated, not by Government interference or by the use of a lot of subsidies, but by more education and assistance in marketing pulp and lumber from small producers.
Pulp companies and large processors have no objection to exporting the end result of what they produce. For some reason, and I suppose it is natural, they would like to have a captive source of supply. They are very reluctant to see small producers get involved, as they used to do, in exporting lumber and even pulp to other countries. The balance of payments and the general business procedures affecting the best interest of this country should be looked at. The federal Government together with the provincial Government should look at some of the captive supply situations that exist in some of the markets in eastern Canada. The federal Government can participate, not only in cost sharing projects and the supplying of expertise but, as was said earlier by my friend, the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) in a question to the Minister, by imaginative taxation policies that provide shelters and opportunities for long-term development in forestry resources under private ownership.
It is also in the interest of the Government of Nova Scotia in considering forestry regulations, and this true of other Provinces I am sure, to refrain from allowing municipalities to pass regulations and bylaws which will affect the proper use and long-term planning of both agriculture and forestry properties. Governments themselves have caused problems because large areas of land have been wasted by highways and power corridors and some large tracts of Crown land have not been utilized in accordance with good forest practices.
When Crown grants were the rule in Nova Scotia, land owners were not restricted to any significant extent and, for the most part, they used the land to its best advantage. Increasing limitations on the use of forest land, either for bureaucratic convenience or to further satisfy the interests of Governments which have become ever more intrusive and manipulative have, to a large extent, eroded the landowner's rights to the point where it is now an exaggeration to say that an owner can truly call himself a freeholder of property. Pretty
May 30, 1983

soon he will simply be a tenant subject to the arbitrary interference of either the municipal or provincial Governments.
I repeat that the best thing that could happen for the encouragement of forestry and for the highest and best use of forest lands in the Province of Nova Scotia would be more opportunities for the purchase of small tracts of Crown land by Nova Scotians, or indeed by Canadians or even people from other countries who wish to have the satisfaction of owning a piece of our Province and treating it properly, using proper practices of silviculture and forest management. Anyone who has a sincere interest in owning a few acres of forest land will treat it properly.
I have always been against the practice that has grown up in recent years of Governments acquiring large tracts of land. As one would really not expect, Governments made it very difficult for its own people to obtain access to it for the leasing of a few acres for firewood harvesting, or for building a cottage by a lake or stream. I cannot understand why the Government did not learn and does not continue to profit from the past experience, because people who truly care about forestry are not liable to be careless with matches. They are not liable to cut down all their trees. In fact, history has shown that people who own their own land are far more careful of it and take far better care of it than do people who lease timber rights from the Government and leave a wasteland behind them by clear cutting the land. In many cases, that land would have been better off if it had been burned rather than logged in the way that I have described.
It has been said that people who plant trees do not think of themselves. Certainly the long-term nature of forestry cannot be over-emphasized. The original stands of high quality timber, the black spruce and white pine, oak and ash, and other original growth that once stood in the forests of Nova Scotia, must be reseeded or replanted now. I sometimes think that the ravages of the spruce budworm might have been Mother Nature's way of removing a very undesirable and inferior type of growth that perhaps grew up simply because of an accident of history.
Your Honour probably does not know that by the turn of the century, there were over 60,000 small farms in the Province of Nova Scotia. When the industrial expansion in the United States began to accelerate, the decendants of the people who had labouriously cleared that land, sometimes by hand, decided that their fortunes would be improved if they went to Chicago, Boston or Los Angeles to work. As a result, when they left, nature quickly reclaimed all of those lands that were so labouriously cleared. What grew up, however, was not the original growth but generally a mixture of alder bushes and what we call cat spruce, as well as wild cherry and other waste trees.
This provides another possible area of research which could benefit areas like Nova Scotia where some of the land is marginal for farming in any event, but this land has demonstrated that it can grow good forests. I believe that in some cases, soils of this type, besides being planted with the original
Supply
forest, could be planted with fast growing trees like aspen which would provide a ready source of wood alcohol or ethanol. Other countries have started to do this. Brazil is one of them. There is no reason why, with some imagination, parts of the land of eastern Canada could not in effect be re-ruralized by the growth of certain types of fast growing trees that could quickly produce ethanol. Certainly that would be a far better and higher use of the land than allowing it to lie fallow as it is now in some cases.
Another thing that I would like to see the federal and provincial Governments do, Mr. Speaker, is to become more interested in the highest and best use of timber. I see that my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker. Too often I have seen the scarce good timber that still remains in Nova Scotia ground up for pulp instead of converted into lumber which is a much more worth-while resource.
In any event, it is pretty obvious that with our traditions and respect for the ownership of land and in appreciation for what forestry meant to us in our early years as a Province and, before that, as a successful colony, we should be very conscious of the help that the federal Government can be to us. As a joint project, we should all work together so that both Governments can do their share, not by making subsidies available, not by being intrusive, but by providing expertise in research, scientific development and marketing for this industry.

Mr. Speaker, I direct a short question to the Hon. Member which is again on the theme that 1 had raised before. In the Hon. Member's Province and, of course, in the adjoining Province of New Brunswick, there are many native people, and of course this particular resource is of great interest to them. In my own area there are large bands such as the Nimpkish people of Alert Bay, the Helltsuk people of Bella Bella, the Kitasoo people of Klemtu, the Nuxalli people of Bella Coola, the Mowachaht people of Gold River and Sechelt, the Sliammon people of Powell River, and each one of these particular groups of people either has access to large reserves of timber or they actually have band timber available. Yet there are no Government programs that provide any meaningful assistance to allow these people to develop those resources, balance out and strengthen and diversify their economy.
It is my understanding that the same limitation exists in the region of the country for which the Hon. Member was putting forward a case on development of the forest industry. I would ask why he has not chosen to stress this very important, albeit small, area of forestry development and what he would be prepared to do as an individual to bring this case forward quickly with the Government to try to make sure that native people are in fact given access to forest industry in a meaningful way.

Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent question. I am pleased to say to my colleague that I can see no reason why, in the Province of Nova Scotia, some of the Crown lands which are under provincial ownership could not be made available to some of the native people who, as he knows, are mostly Micmac. In my own constituency, there is a small band

May 30, 1983
Supply
which is desperately in need of access to some timber. 1 think that it is an excellent initiative.
If there was ever a case for an affirmative action program in terms of giving native people a chance to take part in the lands and forest industry where they have a special feel for the forest and nature or for giving them access to Crown lands, I think that this is a valid one. It is very tough to run an equal opportunity program and an affirmative action program at the same time, and I am pretty sceptical of some of them, but this is one affirmative action program that I would support. From time to time, I have spoken to the Government of Nova Scotia about it.

Mr. Speaker, I think that this is an interesting bit of progress made by Members of the House. I heard the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) and several Members of the Opposition speak on this. I know where this Party stands but I wonder if the previous speaker, whose inclination seems to be as clear as my own, would be prepared to join with this Party and press the Minister of Supply and Services, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) to develop quickly, before the House adjourns, a specific program to aid our native people with access to and the development of their forest resources.
I wonder, also if it would be possible for the three groups in the House to move on that question. Would the Hon. Member be prepared to consult and work toward that goal before we rise in June?

Absolutely, Mr. Speaker. I realize that the Hon. Member has a sincere interest in this, but he should not be giving the impression that only he and his Party favour such an initiative. I would be very pleased to join with him.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to do part of my speech in French, to show Francophones that there are a few Newfoundlanders who realize that French is more important in Canada than Chinese.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, another very important reason is that when my fellow Newfoundlander, my dear friend the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), is chosen as the new Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, he will need someone who can understand French, translate it into English and then translate the English into Newfie!

I begin my few remarks without wanting to disturb my good friend, the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). For the information of the Hon. Member for Brampton-George-town (Mr. McDermid) I simply said that I fully support the
candidacy of my compatriot and dear friend, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). I recognize that he will have many needs once he becomes, as he surely will, the Tory Leader.
I want to begin by saying how I commend the Opposition for choosing forestry for today's debate. Just when I was about to lose completely all my confidence in the Official Opposition, it came through with something sensible. I suppose that is exactly what we can expect from the eminently sensible Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle).
Forestry is big business in the Province which I represent. I grew up a couple of miles from a pulp mill and a dozen miles from the giant paper mill at Grand Falls. It is now owned and operated by Abitibi but was formerly known as the Anglo Newfoundland Development Company in the great days of British imperialism. I worked for AND for two weeks as a woodcutter in the days before chainsaws. I might say that my career was cut a little short. I was living in camp and therefore the cost of my board and lodging was deducted from my wages. At the end of the first pay period I discovered that I owed money to the company, so I concluded very quickly that my destiny was elsewhere than in the forest industry.
You should have worked harder.
That is free enterprise.

They are a live bunch opposite today, Mr. Speaker. That is a sign of a restful weekend. They would be more tired if they visited their constituencies more often and came back here for a rest.
The electoral riding of Burin-St. George's-
Oh, oh!

That is on the south shore, on the South Coast of Newfoundland, I say to my friend from Brampton-Georgetown. I am willing to wager, Mr. Speaker, that sometimes the Hon. Member does not talk; that there are actually times when he does not babble all the time.
In the riding that I represent, Burin-St. George's, forestry is a very important component in two particular parts of the riding, St. George's in the western part of the riding and Bay D'Espoir in the central part of the riding.
I take particular interest in the resolution set down by the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River. I would invite him to reflect on the wording of the resolution, particularly in light of the comments made in the House today by his colleagues, the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). I thought those two gentlemen were careful to put some distance between themselves and the resolution. 1 thought they were wise to demonstrate that they really did not support the strong condemnation in the wording of the resolution. I was encouraged to hear from them and from the Hon.
May 30, 1983

Member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) that not all Government initiatives in the forest industry are wrong. Those Hon. Members voiced a feeling that is widespread in the forestry sector.
The federal Government's contribution to a healthy forest industry in this country has been and continues to be impressive. Under the leadership of the Minister of the Environment and the Assistant Deputy Minister for the Canadian Forestry Service, Mr. Les Reed, we have made great strides in the last few years in lending adequate and appropriate support to the forest industry.
I listened with great interest to the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich. He continues to confuse me somewhat, not by his brilliance, although he has that and is unquestionably a very able man, but by the inconsistency he brings to the debate. Usually I hear him lamenting what in his view is the considerable extent of Government intervention in private enterprise. Today, however, he makes a case, and a very good case, for even more intervention. I think particularly of his comments relating to reforestation. He talks rather passionately about the need for more involvement of Government in that particular area. That is not consistent with his other remarks about Government involvement. I am pleased to see that in this particular area he recognizes that if our forests are to be properly conserved and regenerated, continued and active federal Government involvement will be required.
1 want to draw the attention of the House to a number of important initiatives taken by the Government. Perhaps the highest profile is enjoyed by the forestry agreements between the Government of Canada and the several Provinces. These agreements are now in place and most of them will shortly come up for renegotiation. I have no doubt that the Government's commitment in that particular area will continue. Over a five-year period under these agreements the Government's commitment is in the order of $750 million.
The Minister of Supply and Services referred to the water bombers, the CL-215, which represent another $150 million federal money. I could mention the job-creation activities in the order of $200 million, the forestry school for $15 million, research and development for $5.5 million, the initiative in the Gaspe which is another $20 million. With those figures 1 have enumerated amounts which total about $1.25 billion. It is important to keep the mandate of the federal Government in mind in this particular respect.
It is important to keep in mind that almost any initiative which the federal Government takes in the forestry area has to be hand in glove with those of the provincial Governments. Having said that, I stress that the federal Government does have important responsibilities in this sector in so far as regional development is concerned, as well as employment growth, export development and its impact on balance of payments. The whole research and development area as it relates to forestry is one in which the Government must continue to show new leadership.
Supply
I suppose if one were to state concisely the over-all mandate and responsibility of the federal Government in this area, it would be in terms of the wise use and conservation of the renewable resources of the forestry industry, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the most important way in which Canada can become more competitive in this sector is with an abundant supply of high quality timber at an economical price. The forest renewal policy of the Government is designed to offset threatened timber supply problems and thereby, in the long run, to reduce costs.
There is more to the forest sector, Mr. Speaker, than simply planting seedlings and tending the new crops. There is a human resources program already implemented by this Government which provides for high quality manpower. Some of the components of that particular human resources program include summer jobs for 300 forestry school students, graduate scholarships for 50 Canada forestry scholars every year, grants to forestry schools for visiting scholars and research contracts, and upgrading of the R and D scientific staff in the Canadian Forestry Service. More than $16 million have been committed by this Government to this program over a four-year period.
Let us take a look now at the expansion of the research and development program in the Canadian Forestry Service. For the year 1983-84, a commitment of $5.5 million has been made to that program. In addition, new and expanded research buildings will soon be started in Victoria, British Columbia, Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, Quebec City and Fredericton, New Brunswick. The reason for proceeding first with high quality manpower and research capacity is that we can better field forestry and make our scarce forest renewal dollars stretch even further if we concentrate on those priorities at the outset.
I would like to speak for a moment on another issue which is important in any discussion of forestry and the forestry industry in Canada, and that is the United States countervailing duty threat against Canada's lumber, and this Government's role in successfully countering that particular threat. It has been 20 years, Mr. Speaker, since Canada has faced such an ominous threat to its export trade as the U.S. countervail action against our soft wood lumber. Fortunately, the countervail threat may now be distinguished, at least put behind us for a moment.
It has been alleged that the Government of Canada has failed to carry out its share of the responsibility for fighting the U.S. industry's pressure. The tension arose because of the severe slump in lumber markets world-wide, but especially in U.S. residential construction which was brought on by high interest rates. Normally, the U.S. customers are pleading for Canadian supplies because they themselves cannot produce more than 60 per cent to 70 per cent of their soft wood lumber requirements in a normal market. Fortunately, the Canadians were supported by the National Association of Homebuilders, the North American Wholesale Lumber Dealers' Association, the International Woodworkers of America, and by many others. Without taking you, Mr. Speaker, through the details of our repsonse to that countervail action, I believe it is important to record that the issue was successfully fought

May 30, 1983
Supply
because all concerned recognized the wisdom of our case and the folly of the U.S. private enterprise case in his particular issue.
I would like to comment briefly on the criticism which was aimed at the federal Government for refusing to pay a part of the cost. First of all, the action by the U.S. people did not involve a charge by the U.S. administration, but rather by a small segment of the U.S. lumber industry. It is traditional that industry bear the main burden of defence, whether it is with respect to steel, potatoes or some other product, in this case, forest products. Second, the Canadian soft wood lumber committee had the expertise to conduct its own defence, and did so with the collaboration of the several Governments involved, the federal Government of Canada and the provincial Governments which were directly affected by this countervail threat.
Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding that rather ominous threat to which I have made brief reference, the forestry relations between Canada and the United States have been quite positive and, I believe, mutually supportive over many years. One could take a number of examples. Perhaps the first which comes to mind is the CANUSA agreement, the Canada-U.S. Forestry Agreement, which in particular embraces a co-operative research effort on the spruce bud-worm. It is a program from which we have seen some very positive results and some cost-saving benefit to Canada and, I am sure, to the United States. I could mention the collaborative initiative of fire suppression between the two countries. That agreement was signed last year by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) and Secretary Black of the U.S.
For many years there had been some exchange of water bomber aircraft. Much of this was done under rather awkward and hasty arrangements. However, now we have formalized those arrangements and put them in place to facilitate a rapid response to forest fire emergencies, particularly in those areas which are fairly near our border.
I could mention, as another example of U.S.-Canadian cooperation in this area, the supply-demand working group. The U.S. and Canadian Forestry Services are now developing working groups on timber supply and forest products demand. In the area of investment capital, there have been good signs of collaboration. The flow of forest industry capital funds has moved between Canada and the United States with relative freedom. As a matter of interest, foreign ownership of Canada's forest products manufacturing facilities has declined over the past 10 to 15 years from 35 per cent to something less tahn 25 per cent during that period. That change has occurred without any public controversy.
I could mention the area of wood promotion as another example of the kind of co-operation which exists between the two countries, co-operation which is to our mutual benefit. The lumber producers in Canada and the U.S. have worked closely together over the past 15 years in joint trade promotion
activities. The National Forest Products Association of Washington derives one quarter of its annual budget for product acceptance from Canadian lumber producers. The American Wook Council secures 10 per cent of its budget from Canada. In this way, we work together as two countries to counter the threat of competing materials and to improve design standards. The forestry relations which I have described briefly give ample evidence of how closely our two countries are working together at the official level to the mutual benefit of all concerned.
There are many other issues, Mr. Speaker, but I see my time has expired.
