speechtext: Are there Hon. Members wishing to rise to ask questions?

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: Order, please. It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 45, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster)-National Resources-Processing of uranium-Export of concentrate; the Hon. Member for Mississauga South-Finance-Income security investment plan, (b) Potential of small businesses to create jobs; the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy)- Mines and Mining-Closing of Sherritt Gordon Mine at Lynn Lake, Manitoba, (b) Request that tax write-off provisions be changed.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Oberle:
That this House condemns the Government for its neglect of Canada's forests and its indifference to the threat posed to Canada's forests and forest industries by pests, fire, pollution and foreign competition, and calls upon the Government to stimulate the research needed to promote superior growth and diversify export products, and acknowledge its responsibility to protect the Canadian environment and the millions of Canadians whose livelihood depends upon Canada's forest resources.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a question of the Hon. Member on the Government side of the House, who was at one time, I believe, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister concerned with this issue. Given the fact his speech did not include reference to native people and their access to
*


May 30, 1983

the forest industry, although he rattled off a number of figures indicating employment opportunities, can he tell the House how many of the people hired through the initiatives he mentioned have been native people? How many of the research facilities will be targeted toward the natives to aid them in the economic development of native reserves? What kind of native employment targets has the Government developed in the forest industry?
Given the fact that a number of people in this House have indicated their support today for immediate initiatives to make sure that the native peoples have access to the forest resource, would he be willing to support, in co-operation with other Members here and in his own Party, access by native people to the forest resource for the development of something like a native forest development corporation? Or perhaps he would support affirmative action so that companies who receive benefits from the federal Government, such as Crown Zeller-bach, MacMillan-Bloedel and others, hire native people on an affirmative action basis. Would he lend his support to training programs being established for young native people to get into the industry, whether it is in the Canadian Forestry Service, private companies or through Employment and Immigration sponsored programs?
Can the Hon. Member indicate whether or not he is prepared to try to work with other Members of the House to foster co-operation between the Department of the Environment and the Department of Indian Affairs to develop and execute effective programs so as to make native involvement in the forest industry in Canada a reality?

Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to thank the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) for the question. I can support any initiative at the federal Government level which would give fair access to native people to the industry. I can identify with much of the spirit of the question the Hon. Member has put. I have in my own riding an important native community, that of Conne River, on the South Coast of Newfoundland.
Are they Indian?
Yes, they are Micmac Indians, for the benefit of my friend, the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River.
Tell your Minister.

The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) well understands that they are Micmac people. He has given much of his time on a priority basis to seeing that $1 million of federal funding flows to the people of Conne River, despite a rather deliberate and longstanding procrastination by the Hon. Member's political friends, the Tory Government of Newfoundland, who for 22 months blocked that money from going to that community at some considerable pain, discomfort and inconvenience to the native people of Conne River. I am glad he mentioned my good
Supply
friend, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, because the Minister is the reason why I do not have any fear that this Government will continue to address the problem of fair access for native people to various programs.
I started to say a moment ago, before the interjection, Mr. Speaker, that the spirit of the question from the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River is one with which I can identify. But I am a little surprised he feels the need to ask the question because if he looked at the policy of this Government, whether it is in Indian and Northern Affairs, Employment and Immigration or other areas, he would see that what he is asking is reflected consistently in the approach of this Government to the expenditure of funds and employment policies.

Mr. Speaker, the very reason I asked the question today is that, unfortunately and for whatever reason, it has not been part of the speeches of some Members of this House. It has not been part of the priorities and planning of this Government. What 1 suggested, and what other Members have recognized and said today, is that they are willing to commit themselves to try, before this House rises, to put constructive proposals to the Government. I outlined five things that I felt would work. I asked the Member whether or not he would be prepared to work with other Members of this House in a non-partisan way to try to improve the access of native people to the forest industry. It is a fact that since the turn of the century native people have suffered upwards of 90 per cent unemployment. In my area they are dependent on a sole resource, the fishing industry. Without finding fault, laying blame or going back to the past, I would like to see this House look forward to the future, and would the Hon. Member be prepared to offer his services in a non-partisan way to try to achieve this before the House rises?

Mr. Speaker, I thought 1 answered that question in passing earlier. I said I could give my support to any initiative which ensures fair access by native people to employment and other programs underwritten by the public Treasury. That would certainly include working in a nonpartisan fashion, as 1 am known to do on all occasions with the gentleman from Comox-Powell River, my good friends in the Tory Party-
Name one.
-and my equally good friends in the NDP. By all means, Mr. Speaker, I would name many, but I would not want to give them an unfair advantage in the leadership race by so doing.

Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to ask the Minister a question, but as my friend opposite is the spokesman for the Government I will ask him about his private opinion of the Canadair water bomber. I concede it may have a limited use in some areas, but coming as he does from Newfoundland where it is not always possible to find suitable lakes, would he not agree that helicopters are also a very useful way to fight forest fires, sometimes more so than these, some say, obsolete water

May 30, 1983
Supply
bombers? Would he support a representation to his colleague, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) to give the armed services a role in fighting forest fires as a part of their flight training?

First of all, in relation to the preamble of the Hon. Member for Central Nova, I am not a spokesman for the Government. 1 am happy to support the Government because of the excellence of its policies but 1 am not a spokesman for the Government.
Having said that, he invited me to give my private opinion. That I can do very quickly because the technology of the two types of equipment is something I am not very well versed in. I can tell him, though, that our experience in Newfoundland with water bombers has been quite a happy one. We can point to a number of otherwise very grave incidents which have been avoided because we have had those water bombers available. As the Hon. Member knows, they have been used in Newfoundland for many, many years. How their capabilities compare with those of the helicopters he mentioned I have no idea because I am not informed on the respective technology involved.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to enter the debate, but before getting into the technical matters before us I should like to point out that there is a person in this House who has probably done more for forestry in Canada in the last couple of years than any Member sitting in the House, and that is the Deputy Minister, Les Reed, who is fortunately with us in the Gallery today. I am sure he is very interested in hearing the debate today.
Looking specifically at the motion before us which was put forward by my friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), there are a couple of things 1 would like to raise because they have been put in there for very obvious reasons and they raise some concerns with me. He says in his motion that the House condemns the Government for its neglect of Canada's forest. I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that the Government of Canada controls only 1 per cent of the forests in Canada, some 92 per cent falling within the provincial domain and some 7 per cent being in private hands.
1 have some difficulty with another point raised by the Hon. Member, and I am sure he will be able to clarify it in the question period. It is in relation to a constitutional point which he raises toward the end of the motion which states:
-acknowledge its responsibility to protect the Canadian environment-
I recognize that the federal Government has a certain responsibility, but it is certainly my understanding that the domain of the Provinces includes the environment. We can deal with that in terms of acid rain and so on. I am sure he meant it in that light.
I certainly agree with the part of the motion which calls on the Government to stimulate research massively. More research is a crying need and, as we know from the committee
and the excellent work done by Mr. Reed, it is an area where Canada has fallen drastically behind. It is an issue we must deal with very quickly.
While I agree with the theme of the motion, I have found difficulty with it after having gone to the Parliamentary Library to read a copy of the 1979 budget of the Hon. Member and his Party. The only references to forestry that are even close are to sparkling wine and pickles. The word "forestry" does not even appear in the entire Tory budget of 1979. Therefore, it is evident that in recent times the Tories have not held forestry in as high esteem as pickles and sparkling wine.
Let me talk about British Columbia for a moment, a Province which is of equal importance to myself and to the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River. I am concerned about the provincial sphere there where, in recent years, a fund has been set up to deal with silviculture and replanting. I believe there was approximately S230 million in that fund which was gathered from the forest companies. Unfortunately, it has all been spent on the big gas bag in Vancouver, B.C. Place, and northeast coal. Unfortunately for us and future generations of Canadians, and British Columbians, those hundreds of millions of dollars which should be going toward future forests have disappeared into other priorities of Mr. Bennett's Party, the copatriot party of my hon. friend for Prince George-Peace River.
I have another concern which I am sure the Tories will deal with. That concern is log export. During the last number of years it has reached epidemic proportions in British Columbia. We now see entire pages of logs for sale from companies such as Standing Green, Hemlock, Balsam, Spruce, Cypress and others, by companies such as Macblo, Canadian Overseas and Crown Zellerbach. They are all trying to sell off our future heritage.
A very excellent paper was written by the British Columbia local of the International Woodworkers of America. It concerns the number of jobs that will be lost by the year 2000 as a result of present levels of export. We are now looking at losing about 30,000 jobs by the year 2000 simply from the logs that are being exported now.
Let me quote from a recent article in the Vancouver Sun. It says:
Shortage of Asian timber have also created a high demand for North American logs in the Far East but companies must prove the logs are surplus before they're approved for export. Shipments of uncut B.C. logs have jumped to 724,000 cubic metres during the first eight months of 1982, more than two per cent of the provincial harvest, compares with 591,000 cubic metres during the same period last year, about 1.5 per cent of the B.C. harvest.
1 do not hear any Members from the Government side, the Tory Party or particularly from the Social Credit Party trying to deal with that. It is a very real issue. While it is free enterprise and those logs can be sold now, the logs will go to Japan or Indonesia and the jobs are there instead of in Canada. I think this country and the Province of British Columbia must very soon adopt a policy of no raw log export, because those jobs are for ourselves and future Canadians.

May 30, 1983

Let me deal with a point which has been raised continuously during the debate today by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly). It is in relation to the very important matter of the high levels of non-involvement by native people in the forest sector, not only in B.C. but across Canada. I would have hoped that this motion would have included that, but 1 think that, through the solicitation and questions and very positive responses from the Official Opposition and the Government, we will see some new policies coming forward in Parliament. Perhaps in the next Speech from the Throne we will see some major steps taken in terms of accessing native people to the forest industry in terms of research and development jobs, forest tenure, training, affirmative action with existing corporations in the industry as well as direct industrial development for many of the small rural communities. Many of these communities are similar to those shared by my colleague from Comox-Powell River and other colleagues from British Columbia.
Let me deal with the Environment Canada publication entitled "Policy Statement:	A Framework for Forest
Renewal". This is a good document which was produced last fall in Ottawa. I believe it gives us an idea of the analysis of the federal Government about where the forest industry is going and what problems exist. It points out the following:
The total value of shipments exceeded $23 billion in 1981. Forest products make up one-seventh of all manufactured goods in Canada. The share runs as high as 30 percent in New Brunswick and 50 per cent in British Columbia. Forest industry exports reached $13 billion in 1981, or 16 percent of the total. The forest industry and its employees paid over $3 billion in taxes and resource revenues in 1979, of which 43 percent was federal and 57 percent provincial.
I will come back to those two figures in a moment when I get to the table in this document.
This document goes on to state that directly and indirectly this industry provides one million jobs in Canada. It goes on to say:
As an employment generator among the primary resource sectors, the forest sector ranks first or second in 10 out of 16 economic regions in Atlantic Canada, in 8 of Quebec's 10 economic regions and in all 6 of those of Ontario. In British Columbia the forest sector is first in 8 regions and second in only 2 where mining and smelting dominate.
I think it gives us some indication of the reason why this debate is so important. 1 was interested to note, after reviewing the last 10 or 15 years of debates in the House of Commons, that it is very rare that any forestry matter is raised in the House of Commons even though it is the largest industry in Canada. In terms of balance of trade and actual job creation, it far exceeds the petroleum sector and agriculture combined. Those are two subjects which are frequently debated in the House, but rarely is that kind of profile given to forestry or consideration given to the steps that should be taken with respect to the forest industry. These steps should be taken particularly by the Government and, as I pointed out, by new Governments in office when the word "forest" or "forestry" fail to appear anywhere in its budget.
Let me continue to read from the same document. It says:
This sector has the potential to provide additional employment for approximately 100,000 workers, of which one-quarter could be in forest renewal. The
Supply
potential also exists to double foreign exchange earnings, increase timber sale and tax revenues, and contribute to regional development aspirations.
It is quite clear that a signal is coming from the industry that it wants to double its revenue at a time in British Columbia, for example, when the forest service has indicated that we are very quickly approaching a 20-year falldown effect. If we continue to cut at present rates without some kind of very substantial thinning, silvicultural and replanting process, we will run out of trees and actually be forced in a little more than a decade from now to reduce cutting rather than increase it.
The paper makes some interesting points with respect to the timber supply situation. It states:
In effect, we mined the virgin forests and gave too little thought to the future crop. Forestry is now in a critical transition stage where mining must give way to systematic forest renewal and harvesting.
I very much agree. I know the writer of those comments. I think they are very true and something which this House must deal with. It goes on to say:
World demand for pulp and paper is expected to grow by 3 percent annually for the next 2 decades, whereas demand for lumber and other wood products should increase by about one percent annually. However, market opportunities mean little if timber supply cannot be augmented.
The limits are in sight for premium softwood sawlogs-
We are aware of this, but British Columbia still exports three quarters of a million cunit of our No. 1 logs offshore. It does this knowing full well that an accurate and undisputed study conducted by the workers in the Province point out that it will mean the loss of 30,000 jobs. Yet nothing is done in British Columbia. I do not hear any federal Tory Members from British Columbia publicly saying that this kind of practice should be stopped.
The paper continues:
-in many locations and supplies of larger, higher quality hardwood logs have been largely depleted. Pulpwood shortages are emerging in communities across the country. Only a fraction of our forests are being managed for sustained production, even today. In most cases the timber resource is renewable, both promptly and adequately, only if action is taken immediately following harvest or natural calamity.
That means that if a fire has gone through the area a replanting process should be undertaken immediately. If it is clearcut, no time should be wasted. As we know, literally hundreds of thousands of square kilometres in Canada that have been harvested since the turn of the century are sitting idle and not returning in the type of soft or hard wood that forest companies and various forest specialists expected they would. In early 1980, CCREM, which is the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers, endorsed a target. The target was a level of 210 million cubic metres by the year 2000, or approximately 40 per cent above the harvest in 1981. The point which we must consider is that with the present practices in Canada and the present rate of harvest with which we are involved, we will simply never be able to achieve the levels which have already been endorsed by Environment and Resource Ministers.

May 30, 1983
Supply
The report goes on to touch on three aspects. One involves forest renewal. That is something which the House must debate extensively. Another is closer utilization of the existing forest in terms of fibre supply, recycling and all the rest. That must be done very soon. There must also be better protection from fire, insects and disease. 1 think all Hon. Members of the House are aware of the fact that far more forest is lost to disease and fire than is actually harvested in this country.
Although the Government side has moved on a few water bombers and a few techniques here and there, there must be a really substantive change in forest policy, not only in terms of the kinds of equipment provided, but as well, rather than continuing to pursue monoculture in terms of the forest sector, we must go back to the diversified forest. This is important because of the long distance crowning effect of certain kinds of fires and the massive movement of certain kinds of pests. There are problems which simply have not been alleviated by chemical spraying. We must move very quickly to some kind of integrated pest management approach whereby we start studying, more intensively, the biological side of controlling pests. I know it is something the Canadian Forestry Service is considering. However, having suffered massive reduction in staff for 15 years, it will be a long process, as touched upon by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts). In the last three years the problem has increased about 10 per cent. We need a massive increase in the availability of highly qualified technical forestry staff to deal with the questions involved in returning to a diversified forest, silviculture problems and pest control.
The report goes on to point out that current expenditures on forest renewal by senior Governments and industry are believed to be on the order of $300 million annually, but that an expected total annual expenditure of $650 million will be required by all parties simply to deal with the present problems. It breaks it into two parts. Basically, planting must be increased by about two and half times, from 200,000 hectares to 500,000 hectares, with genetically superior seedlings. In terms of silviculture treatment, weeding, spacing and fertilizing, that must be increased by a power of 400 per cent, from
100.000	hectares to 400,000 hectares annually. That involves a cost of $300 million.
An area in the report which gives me concern, which I am sure is shared by my friend, the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River, is that an expenditure of only $50 million per year is proposed in the report to deal with the backlog of idle forest land. That would bring in only about another
100.000	hectares a year. With the enormous backlog we have,
I think Parliament must make a much stronger move in getting a base fund into our national budget to deal with the backlog problem.
Some Provinces, such as British Columbia, have been using their replanting and silviculture funds for other purposes. Before they are given any comparable funds from the federal Government for reforestation, they should be encouraged, through whatever means possible, to ensure that their own
programs are in order. There should be at least 20-year plans operating, as has been recommended in another part of the report.
The concern which I believe stimulated today's debate comes from the table on page 5, where we see the federal involvement, which has in fact been zero for many years, going to $50 million last year, which was really a shift of DREE funds, only rising to $130 million by 1987 in terms of overall forestry, out of $650 million. Whereas the federal Government's involvement was 37 per cent last year, it means that by 1987 it would drop to 20 per cent, an effective drop of 50 per cent. However, those figures are somewhat difficult to deal with unless one takes them in their proper context. In 1980, for example, the federal and provincial Governments took about $3 billion in taxes directly and from resource revenue, of which 43 per cent went to the federal Government and 57 per cent went provincially.
A myriad of studies have been done, and it is evident that only five cents out of every dollar taxed by the federal Government from the forest sector, whether directly in taxes or from income taxes or resource revenue, has ever gone back into the forest sector. This is a hideous state of affairs, because we have learned from other studies that we are getting into a massive fall-down situation in terms of inadequate supplies of wood. Earlier today I raised this question with the Minister of the Environment, but I do not think his response hit the nail on the head. He tried to fudge around on the issue, saying that UIC Section 38 and DOE support are not included in the 1987 projections because all those agreements are yet to be negotiated.
The House should be considering putting a very substantial sum before the House in terms of a base funding, permanent and perpetual funding, basically receiving a good chunk. Rather than having a situation where five cents out of every dollar goes back to the forest sector, let us ensure that 50 per cent plus goes back in terms of research and development, replanting and silviculture, and in terms of an integrated approach to recycling, getting native people involved in the industry, and so on.
I note that 1 do not have much time left in which to speak, but I would like to touch upon a couple of points with regard to recycling, something which is not included in the motion. However, the House must consider the matter if we are to discuss coherently the problems in the forest sector. It is not only a matter of having a proper study but also of considering the problems now being created at landfill sites, basically as a result of wood fibres in various forms, whether they be paper bags, cardboard, boards or whatever. Following a thorough and balanced assessment, we should consider the feasibility, benefits and costs of using recycled fibre, not only in the pulp industry but also in terms of biomass for electrical production, heat production, and so on.
A few moments ago I mentioned the need to change our ideas from monoculture to a more diversified and mixed forest, not only to help reduce insect and fire outbreaks, but also so
May 30, 1983

that we may more appropriately utilize our soils and forest lands.
There is an abundance of information I would like to put on the record, but I would like to make one final point taken from a recent forestry publication. It points out that of the 800,000 hectares of timber the industry harvests each year, a mere one quarter is artifically replanted or seeded. Given that, another one quarter or so will regenerate reasonably well on its own. The depressing sum is that only half of the cut forest each year has a prayer of one day returning. Added to that was the current rash of forest fires in 1980, the worst fire season in 50 years. The area burned was five times the area harvested.
Parliament has a big job and I think it is a non-partisan issue with which we should deal more effectively than not even mentioning it in the 1979 Tory budget or in terms of the paltry sums which have been allocated for far during this Parliament.

I am very interested in the suggestion of the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) that this is such an important matter for the country and that it should be nonpartisan, then jabbing in the statement at the beginning and end of his speech that there was nothing concerning it in the Tory budget. 1 will address that subject when I am given an opportunity to speak in the House.
1 am also interested in the Hon. Member's condemnation of the exporting of whole logs from B.C. to Japan. I think I heard him properly. I would not want to be unjust. I would like to ask him if he is not aware that there are at least four categories, fallers, buckers, truckers, sawmill workers and longshoremen, involved in the forest industry out in B.C., and that when the market collapsed before cut lumber was out of our sawmills, not only were these sawmill workers out of work, but the fallers and buckers, the truckers and longshoremen were also suffering, and that many logs were cut and fallen, particularly up in the Squamish area, and they could not get to market unless they were taken to market and sold as logs. Is he against that type of activity? Is he against a market activity which keeps the fallers, the buckers, the truckers and the longshoremen at work?

I am glad to have an opportunity to address those two questions. I hope the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) does have a copy of the 1979 budget. I have read it through and I would be interested in learning where forestry is referred to. On the second point, in terms of the export of raw logs, as I said, an abundance of studies have been conducted. The present escalating levels of raw log export from British Columbia will mean the actual loss of 30,000 jobs, right from fallers, buckers, haulers, loaders, shippers to the sawmill workers, that will all go down the tube because logs are being exported now. Those are No. 1 logs which are being exported.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member mentioned that with logs being exported 30,000 jobs will be lost. 1 am suggesting 30,000 jobs would not be lost on the export of the
Supply
logs. There is no market for them, yet those logs were fallen and lying in the bush. I suggest to the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) that it is far better to have those other three categories at work and the harvest of logs that was lying on the ground shipped to markets which can use the logs than to let it all go to pot.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am not completely sure whether the Hon. Member for Capilano has all his facts straight. If he would look in some of the more recent copies of The Sun of Vancouver, 1 think he would see that most of the logs which are being offered for sale are standing green.
That would be a great research facility.

I hear an Hon. Member saying that that would be a great research facility. It is the only place in which we find the offers for sale published. They are standing green. They are in the bush. They have not been cut down yet. If we had the wood being processed, either through a pulp mill or through a sawmill, we would have the thousands of jobs at the other end rather than just the front-end jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions for the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). Sometimes it is unfortunate that we cannot call upon the people sitting in the Gallery. I would like to recognize the presence of Les Reed who has just left, thus I will not embarrass him. Had it been possible for Mr. Reed to participate in the debate, he would have probably said that my colleagues and I have had very serious discussions with the Minister and with departmental officials to do precisely what Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party are suggesting. Indian people throughout the country deserve a share of the economy which is generated by the forest. They should first be encouraged on their own reserves and then on public forest lands to develop their economies and start rebuilding their lives from there.
My question for the Hon. Member concerns the statistics which he quoted. He said that the federal Government owns only 1 per cent of forest lands in Canada. 1 can forgive his ignorance because it is probably a statistic which he read from the forestry department or in The Sun\ that would explain it more. The fact is that federal lands include Indian lands throughout the country. Federal lands south of the 60th parallel exceed in geographic size the Province of Nova Scotia. Most of the Indian lands are heavily wooded, some with commercially viable timber. Federal lands also include parks. While we do not cut timber in parks, the woods in our parks are a very important social asset and of course require the very tender care and attention of the federal Government, no one else.
Going to the Territories, the Hon. Member is totally ignorant because there is all kinds of commercially viable timber in the Territories and in Yukon. Of course it is difficult to get to, but if we think a hundred years ahead, we will realize that there are all kinds of land which would be marginal for agriculture but could be planted today with sufficient foresight and forward planning.

May 30, 1983
Supply
I know that this is not so much a question, but from time to time the Hon. Member needs a little enlightenment, as do all Members in the NDP, so I thought I would take this opportunity to provide him with that short enlightenment.

Mr. Speaker, I am always glad to have an opportunity to respond to high-rolling, tough questions like that. My perception has always been that Yukon and the Northwest Territories are lands basically under their own control. I recognize that they are a federal jurisdiction. However, I was quoting from an excellent article, which 1 recommend the Hon. Member read by Roy McGregor who was the Ottawa editor of Today magazine. It reads:
But not in Canada, where it has never been clear just who might hold over-all responsibility. The federal Government once laid claim to the forests, but by 1930 the Provinces had been given most of the control, and today the Provinces own approximately 92 per cent, private sources 7 per cent, and the federal Government a mere I per cent.
I agree with the Hon. Member on his earlier comment. I would sincerely like to see more involvement of native people in the industry. I was glad to hear the comments of other Hon. Members of the House who would also like to see that proceed because unemployment among native people in Canada is still tragically at about 90 per cent. Something very serious has to be done very soon.

Mr. Speaker, I have another brief question. Would the Hon. Member for Skeena undertake, or should I do it myself, to enlighten the author of the article from which he quoted, because he is obviously as ignorant as he was?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) quite rightly pointed out that the volume of timber lost annually to disease and to pests exceeds by many times the volume of timber lost by forest fires. Several months ago when we discussed in the Chamber the Pesticide Act, a number of Members of the New Democratic Party said that we should cease and desist from the use of pesticides, especially those applied by air. If the position of the New Democratic Party is that we should not use pesticides, how are we supposed to control disease and pests in Canadian timber lands?

I recommend that the Hon. Member read some of the studies which have been done on the chemical spraying program carried out in the Maritimes. It is now quite clear that the majority of that spraying has been quite useless. It simply has not stopped the ravages of the various species of pest which very quickly became reasonably immune to spraying. The Canadian Forest Services entered into a very interesting program which I support. Unfortunately, people such as the Hon. Member who asked the question would not be interested in learning anything about natural biological forms of pest control. There is a very interesting and important bit of work being done right now where a natural pest has been dropped and is being allowed to breed to take over some of the pests that are parasitizing forests in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I also would like to ask the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) a question. Has he ever heard a definition of economic viability of timber which excluded all consideration of the distances to market and the costs of transportation? I was absolutely astounded by the question and the apparent definition of the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) a few moments ago when he said that the Arctic was full of economically viable timber but that of course it was too far from the markets to be sold. Has the Hon. Member ever heard such a definition of economic viability? It leaves me absolutely flabbergasted.
No, I have not, but I hope the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River does not have anything to do with writing forestry policy for the Tories.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to see the motion before the House today. I do not agree with the negative aspects of the motion of the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), but I believe the topic is one that should be debated in the House of Commons in view of the importance of the forestry industry to Canada. Not only is it important to the entire country, but it is of special importance to northern Ontario, an area which I happen to represent. In fact, it employs some 70 per cent of the region's manufacturing work force throughout northern Ontario. Throughout the Province of Ontario, 160,000 jobs are provided directly and indirectly by the industry. In fact, 17 per cent of the nation's export trade or $14.8 billion was earned from the forestry industry in 1980. Indeed, throughout the country there are some 310,000 workers directly or indirectly engaged in that industry. I am told that there are some 300 communities with the forestry industry as their sole industry. We do not have to look very far to see that this industry is very important to our country. In fact, new capital and repair expenditures in 1981 from this industry were estimated to be $4.5 billion, representing some 20 per cent of new manufacturing investment. Therefore, this industry is very important to every Canadian It is important to note that many industries are contracting in job opportunities. I am told that, with the potential in this industry, if we put in place the reforestation, research and further expansion and development of this industry, we can create some 100,000 new jobs.
On the first weekend of February this year, the northern Ontario caucus sponsored a conference in Thunder Bay entitled "Focus on Forestry". The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters) and Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) chaired that conference. Some six Cabinet Ministers and also northern Ontario Members from both sides of the House attended. We made a very intensive study of the whole forest industry. We have been hurting during the past year because of the economic slowdown in North America. However, we wanted to look at the immediate problems of the industry and at such things as research.
May 30, 1983

We had people attend from the Great Lakes Forest Research Laboratory in Sault Ste. Marie. We wanted to look at infrastructure and the needs of the future. We spent a great deal of time talking about reforestation. I chaired the subcommittee working on reforestation. A very important discussion took place there. I want to spend more time talking about that this afternoon.
As well, we talked about trade, transportation and other aspects of the forest industry. A number of important recommendations and representations will be coming forward to the Government from that conference. The discussions we had at that conference on reforestation was of particular importance.
1 am very conscious of it because during the past seven or eight years we have put in place throughout Canada a massive new pulp and paper and sawmill capacity.
In my own constituency of Algoma, historically at Blind River we had the largest white pine sawmill operation east of the Mississippi River. During the thirties, forties and early fifties, that sawmill could produce some 28 million boardfeet of lumber a year. It went above that on a few occasions, but that was the average amount of production. Some 700 or 800 people were involved in the manufacturing and forestry aspect of that operation. It was the largest in eastern Canada.
The Rural Development Incentives Act, put in place in 1969 and the pulp and paper agreement between the federal and provincial Governments offered incentives for the pulp and paper capacity. In Espanola in my constituency, there is a sawmill with a capacity of close to 100 million board feet a year. I am told that when it is completely developed, it will have a capacity of close to 128 million board feet a year. That is larger by at least 100 million board feet of lumber than the historically largest sawmill operation located at Blind River. At the same time, the capacity of the pulp and paper mill at Espanola will have its pulp capacity increased from 500 tons or 600 tons per day to 900 or 1000 tons per day.
Those two developments are in one little area of northern Ontario. These agreements are nation-wide. Clearly the demand for wood fibre has increased. In the sawmill operation example I gave, it has increased fivefold. These economies of scale that are being developed are good. We will be competitive with sawmills throughout the world.
The problem is developing the fibre. A few years ago I had the opportunity to make representation on behalf of a small sawmill operator to the Deputy Minister of Natural Resources in Toronto. When I told him that this small operator wanted greater limits to operate his sawmill, his reply was "Well, we have really gone to the last row of hills". That is true of the whole forest industry. There are no new areas to cut. We have to grow new fibre. We have to stop mining our forests and start farming them on a renewable basis. One instrument for doing that will be the forest management agreements being put in place by many of the provincial Governments.
Ontario has put in place a forest management agreement program. Since 1979 six companies are not only cutting the fibre but are carrying out a regeneration of the fibre. This makes good sense. Obviously there is a public interest in seeing
Supply
additional fibre grown. However, there is an intense interest in that for the individual company, which in many cases has spent hundreds of millions of dollars on pulp and paper and sawmill capacity. By having in place these forest management agreements, it is in their own interest to grow the fibre that will be needed in the years ahead. Under the Ontario arrangement, they will carry out silviculture treatment, road construction, maintenance and the operation of forest limits. It is a 20-year agreement, renewable on a five-year basis.
There are six companies with 131,000 acres of land that have signed these agreements. One is Eddy Forest Products in Espanola. In 1981 it planted 300,000 trees, in 1982 1.6 million trees and in 1983 it will be planting 2 million trees. By 1986 it plans to plant 8 million trees. The company is well ahead of schedule. This kind of agreement is important.
During the last five years, the federal Government has had an important forestry agreement with the Provinces for carrying out regeneration, enhanced forest management, acceleration of reforestation and the creation of employment opportunities. That $82 million program was for construction of forest access roads. When you put in a road, you not only provide an opportunity for harvesting the forest, but you provide an opportunity for management, fertilization, fertilizing the forest for forest fire protection, insect control, and ultimately the use of those in society for leisure, recreation and so on. The forest management agreement between the federal and provincial Governments provides for a nursery expansion program and $11.5 million for planting stock. As well, there is $4.7 million for research and assessment, $2.4 million for silviculture camps and $1.1 million for soil survey. That agreement will come to an end a year from now. It is essential that the two levels of Government put in place a new forest management agreement to reach the objective of the Minister's statement last fall. It was to increase production of wood fibre by 40 per cent over the next decade or so, and that will have to be achieved mostly by forest regeneration.
I want to comment on the concern the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) has about the question of native employment. My own constituency has, 1 think, the second largest Indian band member population in the Ontario region. There has been a very extensive program going on this past year under Section 38 in which $1,121 million has been spent under the Section 38 Job Creation Program on six reserves in my constituency which will be providing 2,702 work-weeks of employment. I think that there are six reserves in my constituency which have sawmills located on them and a number of sawmill operations which are close by.
This is not to say that there is not room for greater opportunity in native employment. Of course, there again the problem of shortage of fibre is faced. Many Indian bands have cut over their existing fibre, and so this Section 38 of the forestry program will provide an opportunity not only for improving these woodlot stands but likewise for planting of seedlings this

May 30, 1983
Supply
year. This program is a co-operative effort between the Canadian Forestry Service and the Canadian Employment and Immigration Commission.
It seems to me that at the Forestry Conference in Thunder Bay, one of the most progressive arrangements that I heard spoken of was that one of the Indian bands had their own forestry management agreement with the Ontario Government and were developing and providing wood fibre for sawmills in the area. It seems to me that there should be an opportunity for that to happen in other areas where Indian bands do not have adequate fibre on their own reserve lands. These bands should have the opportunity to opt into those forestry management agreements which would allow them to operate the license and sell to the operator of the pulp and paper mill or sawmill in their area, unless, of course, they have their own sawmill or pulp operation. It seems to me that there is a real opportunity there.
The proposal to increase employment by 100,000 people, much of it in reforestation, obviously offers a real opportunity. That is not to say that many native people do not already work in pulp and paper and sawmill operations throughout many areas of northern Ontario, but as the Hon. Member has indicated, the unemployment rate on many reserves is much higher than it is off the reserves. So this clearly provides an opportunity that we must expand upon. On several reserves in my own constituency, though, I have seen that the problem is that the limits put on the reserves tend to have been cut over. There must greater reforestation for the long haul.
It occurs to me, Mr. Speaker, that these forest management agreements will have to provide for a number of things if we are to increase the long-term need of greater fibre for the forest products industry. The proposal of the Minister of Forest Resources and Development suggests that spending by Government and industry on reforestation should increase by $300 million to $650 million per year by 1987, that long-term agreements should contain forest management agreements between the private sector and the provincial Government involved, that there should be a provision for transfer of technology, that there should be a provision for intensive forestry and an increase in the input of the provincial Government and the private sector, and that there should clearly be a greater development of private woodlots.
I was interested to hear the announcement of the Special Recovery Capital Projects because I have mentioned the importance of the Great Lakes Forest Research Laboratory in Sault Ste. Marie. That announcement, which was made a couple of weeks ago, in fact included provision for a $13 million expansion and upgrading of the Great Lakes Forest Research Laboratory which serves the Ontario region. It is interesting to note that likewise in other regions $22.5 million was allocated for a new laboratory in Fredricton, $14 million for expansion and upgrading of the facilities of the Pacific Forest Research Centre in Victoria, $10 million for expansion and upgrading of the Laurentian Forest Research Centre in Quebec, as well as $10.5 million contribution for the construction of a forest ranger school on the site of the Maritimes Forest Research Complex at Fredricton. This represents a very
significant commitment by the federal Government, a commitment of some $60 million to these major forestry facilities for research. The federal Government, of course, has a special responsibility in research.
The importance of the purchase of the CL-215 water bombers has been mentioned. That purchase is important not only to keep Canadair viable but it is important to Provinces like Ontario, and especially the northern Ontario region. Much of that activity is based in the City of Sault Ste. Marie and will play an important role in preserving our forests.
It is interesting to note that the Canadair water bomber agreement provides not only for the federal Government to purchase some 20 water bombers, but I believe that it provides for the Provinces to purchase 16 water bombers on a reciprocal basis. If the federal Government spends money on water bomber fleets, the Provinces will do likewise. Similarly, the production of those water bombers probably becomes more economically viable because the agreement offers the opportunity for construction of water bombers for the overseas market. I believe that the announcement indicated that some 20 additional water bombers would be allocated for that. We are looking at a pretty massive project for Canada. It is a project in which I have a special interest because the sub-contractor who is to paint those water bombers is in my constituency of Algoma in northern Ontario. Even though the contract will go to Canadair in Montreal, the spin-off benefits will affect other parts of the country, including that painting subcontract which will help an aerospace facility in northern Ontario.
I would just like to review the Government's role in the establishment of the nation-wide forest fire intelligence and information system which will provide fire control agencies with added water bombing capacity and the opportunity to develop fire management systems to increase the effectiveness of provincial forest fire control operations. This program to which the federal Government is contributing, is centred in Winnipeg and will be a co-operative effort. It is typical of the way that the federal Government is recognizing its responsibility nation-wide, not only in silviculture research but in forest fire prevention and the whole gamut of the forestry industry. The Government is meeting that challenge for the future because of the tremendous importance this industry holds for every Canadian and especially those of us in the resource producing areas.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Do Hon. Members have any questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington).

Mr. Speaker, I think I just have enough time to say what I want to. The problem we are debating today is not new. I compliment my colleague, the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) on the motion because he has brought to our attention once again the serious need for co-operation between the federal level of Government and the provincial level of Government.
May 30, 1983

The same cry was heard in 1925 when C. D. Howe addressed the Royal Canadian Institute saying:
Taking the Dominion as a whole, forestry is much in the same condition as that which Mark Twain once described with reference to the weather: 'Everybody talks about it and nobody does anything about it.'
I think that is why we are debating this Opposition motion today. Canadian forests are a facade. They look plentiful and nourished from the view of an airplane, but in reality they are an asset we are going to lose very quickly if we do not act now.
It is interesting that he was saying this in 1925. As the Hon.. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) keeps telling us, the longer he stays around the more things remain the same. The Government, which has been in power for a long time, really has not addressed this very serious national resource nor has it entered into co-operation with the Provinces to make sure that the total tax resource of the country is used wisely to enable the industry to recover from the position of being overharvested and undernourished.
We may ask why forestry is so important to us. Directly and indirectly it provides one out of every ten jobs in Canada; it provides jobs for 13 per cent of all people employed in manufacturing; it generates over $1 billion in tax revenue for the federal Government; it provides $1 billion in tax revenue for the provincial Governments; forest products exports total $9 billion and account for 18 per cent of all Canadian exports. This one industry contributes more to the federal economy than fishing, mining, fuels and agriculture combined.
Three hundred communities in this country depend on the health and well-being of our forest industries. Canada ranks first in the world in exports, second in forested area and third in forest products. Trees cover 44 per cent of Canada; 4.4 million square kilometres of which are in forest and half of this is harvestable. This is a very serious factor in our timber industry today. I agree with the forecasters who say that in the next 20 years, over 100,000 jobs will depend upon the initiatives we take today. The new Assistant Deputy Minister at the Canadian Forestry Service says that he believes that an immediate, massive and sustained reforestation program can avoid the imminent crisis in the forests. I should like to think that Members of all Parties in the House are prepared to assist him with the muscle, the energy and political pressure he needs to meet his objectives.
Forestry industry consultants, Ted Fellows, says that for at least the next 20 years we will not be able to develop our timber industry as fast as we could have if we had paid more attention to forestry 20 years ago or if we had heard the words of C. D. Howe back in 1925. We have to start immediately and plant like crazy with the best genetic and proved stock that we have. There are a lot of ifs, even if the industry is to start to take a more far-sighted view of the resource base.
It is interesting that we have harvested some 800,000 hectares and replanted only 200,000 hectares while 400,000 hectares have received no regeneration. British Columbia accounts for one third of the world's soft wood lumber exports. There is a world shortage of soft wood fibre. We have to put that into perspective and I hope I will be able to comment on it before I end my speech. About one half of every dollar earned
Supply
in British Columbia stems from forestry and accounts for 42 per cent of total manufactured shipments from that Province.
I will take a risk and say that some of my best friends are foresters. I have travelled the coast. I love the coast and I love the mountains and I love the wilds, but I have seen some terribly stupid things going on out there. I have seen crews of university students hired on special summer programs go out with skid-donkey engines to pull snags and clean streams to allow fish to get up the natural streams to the natural spawning areas. 1 have seen them working in the middle of a stream when suddenly a truck will drive up, take the crew out and leave the donkey engine there. The project is finished with logs still lying in the stream because there is no more money. This is happening everywhere.
Fishery inspectors patrolling the northern waters of British Columbia have sat and had a drink with me. They have told me about the stupidity of not being allowed to take a chainsaw into a stream to cut away a dead fall or a new fall that is interfering with the fish migration. It is in these areas that we seem to be so blind. We cut off budgets where it is terribly important, out in the fields, in the streams, in the area of wildlife, yet we waste and squander so much money here in advocacy advertising, in administration and bricks and mortar. We need planning, reforestation, streams opened up out in the field where the meaningful work is.
When people are put to such work in the summers they feel they have gained something, because they feel the magnitude and majesty of the outdoors. They appreciate the size and scope of the country and know that in their days at university they did something meaningful to earn their education. I should like to see a lot more money from the UIC and from the Department of Employment and Immigration redirected to forestries and fisheries to provide meaningful jobs, not false ones. I get so frustrated with our activities here, Mr. Speaker.
I want to come now to the point made by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) that this Party was in Government for nine months in 1979 but did nothing. I know he will never have that experience so I will point the problem out to him. There is a bureaucratic pipeline, full of planning. The planning takes 42 stages-something gets into the pipeline and comes all the way through. Things in the pipeline normally have to flow through before you get a chance to implement something new. In the meantime you start your planning process and it starts to plug in behind the flow.
In 1978-79, the Government spent $196.1 million on the forestry sector of which $41 million went to the forest service-only $41 million-while $154.9 million was spent by other Departments. That shows the priority that existed with the Fiberal Government prior to 1979.
In 1979-80, the brief period when there was a change in Government, the objectives of the Department were stated in the Estimates as being to promote effective economic management and use of the forest resources of the nation. The objective was to improve the management and sustained economic utilization of the forest.

May 30, 1983
Supply
As a result of the planning and the work that went on in that short nine months in 1979-credit for which goes to the next Government, as is often the case-they get the credit or the blame-the objective in the Estimates was changed as a direct result of work done by our Government. The wording started in 1980-81, and went through to 1983-84, as a result of the change in Government. It was as follows:
To promote and advise on the preservation, enhancement, and wise use of forest resource and terrestrial environment for economic and social benefits; to provide information for policy and program development and co-ordination of federal activities relating to the forestry sector; to carry out research aimed at solving problems and capitalizing on opportunities in all aspects of forestry including forest management, protection, harvesting and utilization; to participate in the evaluation of environmental impacts on the forest resource of forestry practices, air pollutants and major developments; to assess the potential for using forests and trees for energy, chemicals and new products; to provide forestry services and advice to other federal agencies and to promote public awareness of the economic, ecological and social value of the nation's forests.
The Government which was in power for nine months in 1979 set out a whole new area of objectives and a whole new direction. Also, I believe that that Government can take full credit for creating the post of the Assistant Deputy Minister of Forestry and, I believe, in the selection and at least the recommendation of its present incumbent, a man who, I feel, deserves a lot of support from all of us here in the House. I am not going to accept the little jibes of the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), that we did not do anything in that nine months in 1979. We laid some very solid foundation and framework for what could go on, except that it seems now to be stifled with a lack of resources.
I am also troubled, Mr. Speaker, that the Pacific Forest Research Centre has in this Estimate only $775,000 this year. As I have already reported in this speech, the Province is responsible for 33 per cent of the world soft wood lumber exports. There is something very wrong there. Perhaps the free enterprise spirit out in that Province does not require of this Government all the money which some of the other sectors of Canada do. I am not going to stand here and ask the Government to send us more money. Perhaps we do not need it, because 1 believe there are lots of little things which go on to prove that the initiative and innovation of man in small units is far more effective than large bureaucracies which shovel out in wasteful sums the taxpayers' energy and resources.
In the Estimates we have some $94 million forecast expenditures in forestry for 1982-83. Yet the Estimates for 1983-84 dropped by $20 million. Is that not interesting? I notice that contributions to provincial agencies and to persons for development initiatives undertaken under the General Development Agreements and Subsidiary Agreements for the purpose of economic and socio-economic adjustment has dropped from $75 million to $63 million. This does not do us very much good in British Columbia, but we do get out of that $94 million the sum of $50,000 for the Council of Forest Industries of British Columbia. The Council of Forest Industries is a very valuable organization in that it co-ordinates the activities of the industry in B.C. and communicates pretty well and effectively with the federal Government-I would say "all too well" with the
federal Government because it is part of that lobby group of industrialist leaders who arrived down here last week to try to put enough pressure on the Opposition Members to have them support Bill C-155, the Crow Bill. It is that kind of debt which associations like the Council of Forest Industries of British Columbia pick up when they accept money from Governments to sustain their needs. They would be far better off if they kept their independence and their honesty in terms of political force by remaining independent; $50,000 is nothing to the members of COFI out in British Columbia. I would suggest that they do not have to join that type of delegation to twist our arms to submit to something which is totally wrong in principle before the full debate on the Bill is heard.
Grants from the federal Government can control grassroots agencies out in the country. I would warn all of them to be very careful about accepting grants of that nature because they do pick up that kind of leverage, which I believe destroys their true impact and potential which they have as responsible associations.
The Canadian Forestry Service in the 1982-83 Estimates receives $92.5 million. Let us look at how that is distributed. There is $63.8 million for administration of the Canadian Forestry Service. I just heard the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), who is just leaving the chair, talk about all the bricks and mortar which was going to be put into the Department of the Environment, but there is $5 million for capital expenditures and there is $23.7 million in grants and contributions. Administration is two and a half times what they are delivering out in the field where the trees are and where the fish are. There is something very wrong when we can build that type of top-heavy over-burden on anything as important as our forest industry. I notice also that of $346.8 million in grants and contributions, our Province of British Columbia picks up 14 per cent. That is the combination of provincial and federal contributions.
I am very proud to stand in the House and take part in this debate, being from British Columbia, because we are a Province which has done well. Although, I will stand now and criticize our own Province for the fact that in its forest management licences, it has set its inventory far too high. It has included inventory in the higher elevations on the mountains which are difficult to get to and which are causing flooding and water problems and which, generally, has caused an overharvest in the Province which we are having to pay for. However, there are some interesting things happening in British Columbia. I believe we have to recognize, Mr. Speaker, that the world is short of fibre, short of soft wood fibre, and if we can get our act together and not accept the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that co-operative federalism is dead, if we can get back to a sense of co-operative federalism and have the federal Department of Environment work in coordination and co-operation with the Provinces, we can then start to replant, to give the generations of tomorrow some of the strength we are taking from them today in our overspending.
May 30, 1983

There is a tremendous opportunity which we have to serve the future generations by utilizing and making the federal Department of Environment go out in the field and be cooperative with the Provinces so that we can address the real issues of species research. The whole market is changing, Mr. Speaker. Out in British Columbia we have big sawmills collapsing. They will no longer work. The whole market is such now that as we go farther out from the tidal ports, we are moving into smaller more efficient sawmills. One of the greatest things we need now in our industry in British Columbia is a new type of saw. And we can do more of the manufacturing out in the hinterlands and cut down the transportation costs to market. We have a situation in the Okanagan and in the small forest areas now where we are fingerjoining small cut trees, and that is opening up a whole new vista for us.
I am pressured with time here, Mr. Speaker, and I would love to explain what is going on in some of the forest culture. Crews are now going out and trimming the branches off trees for three metres in height in order that down the road, 60 years away, there will be tall, knot-free trees which will have maximum market use in the future. I personally was involved in the research which made the breakthrough for cottonwood farming on the deltas of our rivers out in British Columbia. That was over 25 years or 30 years ago now. We can now start to see the harvest of these cottonwoods. It is now becoming one of the most important areas for manufacturers of fibre products, such as Scott Paper. They are now expanding what we started in a very small way. It is now being expanded to the major river deltas all up through the coast of British Columbia. We have not done that expecting great gobs of money from Ottawa. That original research all came from the private sector which hired people like me to work on those research projects in the field and to make them possible. This type of thing does not come from these bricks and mortar monuments we build here with all these millions of dollars. We must feed it out, give incentives and encouragement into the field. We must allow the Department of Environment and that new ADM to start co-operating with the industry through the Provinces and see if we cannot get a spirit of well-being and growth going in this very important part of our lives.

subtopic: NATIONAL RESOURCES-PROCESSING OF URANIUM-EXPORT OF CONCENTRATE
NATIONAL RESOURCES-PROCESSING OF URANIUM-EXPORT OF CONCENTRATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 20,
1983, I put a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) as follows:
Could the Minister clarify the Government's policy concerning further processing of uranium in Canada? At the present time the Government is spending some $200 million to build uranium refining facilities at Port Hope and
Adjournment Debate
Blind River. However, last summer it exempted a large sale of uranium concentrate from being upgraded in Canada-
I put that question to the Minister because last summer the Government's uranium review panel exempted from further processing in Canada some 1.8 million kilograms of uranium oxide. This decision resulted in the loss of some $10 million in foreign exchange and cost the country some 150 person years of work. All this at a time when we have 1.5 million Canadians unemployed.
My own personal concern is that at the present time in the town of Blind River in my constituency a uranium trioxide refinery is being built at a cost of $130 million. At the same time a uranium hexachloride upgrading facility is being built in Port Hope. We have been trying for a long time to achieve further processing of our natural resources in this country. Yet this large sale of uranium to the United States from Saskatchewan was exempt from further upgrading in Canada.
I understand this came about mostly because the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation put pressure on the Government, saying if it did not exempt this from further processing then the company would lose the sale. Mr. Speaker, that is hard to believe. I understand this uranium was sold for around $17 a pound. Yet Australia will not allow uranium to be sold for less than $35 a pound. So it is just hard to believe that if the federal Government had forced this uranium to be processed in Canada the sale would have been lost.
Even if the odd sale is lost, it seems to me that we should maintain the principle of continuing to process our own uranium. We are going to a lot of trouble and expense to create this processing capacity in Canada and we should not be knuckling under to the pressure of provincial Governments. It is my understanding that they are not only pressuring the federal Government, they are trying to coach other producers in how to avoid further upgrading in this country.
It can be clearly seen how committed the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation is to further processing of our natural resources in this country. I hope the Government will not allow future sales of uranium to leave the country without further upgrading and processing taking place here. Clearly, we do not want go back to being hewers of wood and drawers of water. We want to get the value added to our natural resources. We want to create and keep the jobs in this country.
I hope the Hon. Member responding to my representations today will make a clear statement that uranium will not be exported from this country without further upgrading. We have very efficient facilities for upgrading. We can do it as cheaply as any other country in the world. The Government should reaffirm its policy statement so that everyone will know that it is the policy of the Government of Canada that we carry out upgrading and further refining of our uranium resources in Canada.

May 30, 1983
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATIONAL RESOURCES-PROCESSING OF URANIUM-EXPORT OF CONCENTRATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should say at the outset that the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) has raised this issue on previous occasions, both in committee and in the House. Indeed, he has raised it in his discussions with the Minister and myself as well. I can appreciate his rightful concern.
We are all familiar with the problems in our uranium and nuclear industries. One common element of these problems is that we tend to be working toward conflicting goals. In the case of uranium, we are on the one hand expanding our uranium mining industry, while on the other hand we have placed certain conditions on exports which encourage development of our uranium refinery and conversion businesses. The conversion business presupposes the existence of uranium export contracts. Outright insistence on further processing could lose both the immediate uranium business and the sale of conversion services.
The Canadian Government has always been sensitive to the problems facing the uranium industry. The processing problem was addressed by the then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in early 1974 when he stated:
Uranium will be required to be exported in the most advanced form possible in Canada unless specific exemption is granted by the control agencies.
This position was reaffirmed in the September, 1974, statement on Canadian uranium policy.
The most advanced form presently possible for essentially all of Canada's uranium exports is uranium hexafloride, LiF*in6, and this is likely to be the case for some years. The basic further processing issue is the degree to which Canada should insist on conversion of uranium to UF*in6 before export. If it does so, there is a risk of lost sales. If it does not, it puts at risk its investment in Eldorado's new refining and conversion facilities. It could also compromise its policy of industrial development based on natural resources.
It may be that the exemption issue will not affect a sufficiently large portion of Canada's substantial uranium exports to threaten the further processing policy. However, exemptions could be considered pragmatically on a case by case basis.
From 1973 to 1979, uranium was perceived to be relatively scarce and it was not difficult for Canada to obtain compliance from uranium customers in respect of its further processing policy. The present situation is very different. There is considerable overcapacity and some uranium customers have already contracted for their conversion services.
Canadian uranium producers are finding that the market is soft and that sales prospects are difficult to find and hotly contested. The condition of further processing in Canada is considered onerous by some customers, even if it is imposed only when there is a capacity available and when the Canadian services are competitive. Customers want complete freedom to to shop around for conversion services in a buyers' market.
However, the Canadian Government recognizes the importance of developing its own uranium and conversion business
and does not freely grant exemptions from its further processing policy. The exemptions which have been granted have been made only after careful consideration by Ministers of the facts surrounding the sale.
In conclusion, I would like to reiterate what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) stated in the House on May 20, that the Government of Canada wants to maximize refinery in Canada, but not at the cost of losing uranium sales.

subtopic: FINANCE-INCOME SECURITY INVESTMENT PLAN. (B) POTENTIAL OF SMALL BUSINESSES TO CREATE JOBS
FINANCE-INCOME SECURITY INVESTMENT PLAN. (B) POTENTIAL OF SMALL BUSINESSES TO CREATE JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 27 last, I raised a question in the House with the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) concerning the Income Security Investment Plan filed with the budget. At the outset let me say that we on this side of the House are reasonably happy with the Income Security Investment Plan. We see nothing really dangerous about it. Indeed, the spirit of allowing those who invest in securities to shelter themselves from the effects of inflation, which is really the granddaddy of the production of all capital gains in this country, is a proper activity. Indeed, we would like to see, by and large, capital gains taxes removed from all business investment. However, what we have here is a plan which is very limited in its scope.
I raise the question because the plan is a help to those who are in large businesses which finance in the stock market, but it is of no help whatsoever to small or medium-sized businesses, to family owned businesses or closely held businesses. Most businesses in this country, even large businesses, are not listed on the stock market, nor can they be. This is not because they are relatively closely held. The families and individuals owning the businesses cannot easily accept the problem of turning their businesses into public corporations. These are they very businesses which are dynamic, growing and creating most of the jobs in the country.
The budget we faced on April 19 last was supposed to attack the problem of unemployment. Massive numbers of Canadians are unemployed. The Minister and the Government are looking presumably to the private sector to be the engine of growth, the engine of the supply of jobs. Frankly, the capital gains tax seriously hurts business in terms of encouraging people to invest and to create new opportunity, because with a capital gains tax facing an investor, the zing, the hope of profit, the smell of a go-ahead economy, is to a large extent taken away.
