speechtext:
My friend says "nonsense." I say to Your Honour that what we must do is encourage investment, investment by individuals of all kinds. To wind up with a system which helps only the rich, large corporations which happen to be listed on the stock market, and then only in a very bureaucratic fashion, is just not good enough. If the
May 30, 1983

Government really intended to do something to create jobs, if it really intended to make business investment the kind of thing that was there for the engines of growth about which the Government speaks, then it would have come forward with a plan much broader and much more comprehensive in terms of business investment and the way inflation affects that investment. It has not.
These questions were asked of the Minister of State for Finance. The House should receive an apology from the Government for this Minister. He really does not understand the budget nor the Income Investment Security Plan. His answers can be read in Hansard as reported at page 24897. He went on to speak of the Special Recovery Tax and the $4.8 billion which is to somehow stimulate the economy. But the questions were directly with respect to this investment plan. It is too bad the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) is not more competent. I am hoping we will receive a good response from the Parliamentary Secretary who is certainly far more competent in financial matters than his Minister.
With that aside, it is important that we have a response from the Government to encouraging investment in business, something much more comprehensive than this plan which in some senses is only applicable to people who trade stock rapidly on the stock market. That was the suggestion of Lyman Maclnnis, President of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants. We should have a plan that does not require those who invest in the shares of any business to pay taxes on inflationary gains, or that allows them to deduct losses if there is a tax against a gain.
The present system of capital gains tax is really a tax on inflation. Most of the capital gains on which the Government has collected tax were gains that resulted from inflation. When it comes to business investment, particularly, it is totally improper that that type of gain should be taxed; indeed, we would be far better off in terms of employment and in terms of growth if we did not tax those gains at all.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-INCOME SECURITY INVESTMENT PLAN. (B) POTENTIAL OF SMALL BUSINESSES TO CREATE JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let us put the income investment security plan into its proper context. Let us start with the postbudget analysis in Maclean's magazine wherein it was indicated that business was the big winner in the budget. Following the applause from Maclean's, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in its newsletter in May indicated:
Canadian Chamber reacts favourably to recent federal budget.
It went on to indicate:
With this in mind, it applauded the Minister for recognizing the important role of the small business sector by introducing a number of special tax and other measures that may help to alleviate certain elements of the difficult financial situation faced by small business.
That is a very strong statement which indicates to us that the small business sector, the sector which is not traded on the stock market, has reacted well to the budget as a total package. In fact, the Chamber of Commerce told us that it submitted 30 ideas, of which 24 were approved in whole or in part. The Chamber indicated that it agreed with the budget and viewed it as a win on behalf of small business. It also indicated
Adjournment Debate
that the budget would create investment, business expansion and new jobs.
There are three important tax measures in addition to the ISIP which the Hon. Member mentioned. There is the share purchase tax credit which was worth $240 million in business stimulus. There is the investment tax credit, with special new rules to enrich new investment, and those rules are even better for small business than they are for big business. There are the carryback and carryforward provisions on losses that allow people to obtain refunds on their taxes over the past three years or the next seven years to alleviate loss. These things will let small businesses obtain equity financing, get off debt and get themselves into a much better cash flow situation.
When we set up ISIP we listened to the Lortie Commission and to pre-budget consultations. In fact it was all a breakthrough in effective pre-budget co-operation. Perhaps it is because of that that I can close with a direct quote from the Investment Dealers' Association which indicated that the budget was "a carefully thought-out program to help the private sector in the recovery". I think ISIP has to be put into context, and that small business measures in the budget are one of our strongest points.

subtopic: MINES AND MINING-CLOSING OF SHERRITT GORDON MINE AT LYNN LAKE, MAN. (B) REQUEST THAT TAX WRITE-OFF PROVISIONS BE CHANGED
MINES AND MINING-CLOSING OF SHERRITT GORDON MINE AT LYNN LAKE, MAN. (B) REQUEST THAT TAX WRITE-OFF PROVISIONS BE CHANGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to make further comments to those I made in the House of Commons regarding the proposed closing by Sherritt Gordon Mines Limited of its Fox Lake mine operation in the area of Lynn Lake, Manitoba. One of the questions I asked in the House at that time was directed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I referred to the fact that tax deductions allowed to companies for exploration are actually preventing exploration from taking place in the Lynn Lake area. I asked a supplementary question which was answered by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). I referred to the NEED program and the application which had been put forward by the company.
I wish to explain that the problem facing the residents of Lynn Lake, Manitoba is simply that the company will be closing its present mine in 1985 or 1986. As a short-term project it re-filed a NEED application with the Government on May 11, 1983, as the first application did not meet the criteria. In its request, the company asked for approximately $2.6 million of which Sherritt will pay $1,138,625. The federal Government is being asked for $1,011,575 and the provincial Government $547,200. The Manitoba provincial Government has indicated its support for the second NEED application. That is a good sign. I encourage the federal Government to give this application favourable consideration. It is recognized by the residents of my community that the first application did not meet the criteria of the program. I am glad that, after

May 30. 1983
Adjournment Debate
some consultations, the company has put forward what 1 believe to be an acceptable application.
In the few minutes available to me, I want to talk about the other matter I raised in my question to the Prime Minister. I recognize that in certain circumstances, perhaps not in all, the provisions that allow a corporation to write off either past or future profits against certain exploration costs do not necessarily encourage exploration. I will give the example of the operation of Sherritt Gordon in the Lynn Lake, area.
In that case, Sherritt Gordon does not have the money at this time for exploration. It has not been able to do much exploration in this area over the last few years. As a result, it has not been able to find a new ore body for its present copper-zinc operation in that area. The provincial Government has offered to come in on a joint venture whereby it would receive some equity control of that operation in return for doing exploration in that area. It is the same kind of negotiating for a contract that would exist between Sherritt and any other private enterprise operation.
The reason the company has given for not accepting the offer of the provincial Government, an offer which could save jobs and businesses in the town of Lynn Lake, is that the federal tax provisions for exploration are so good for private enterprise, that sometime in the future it may get a better deal if it forms a partnership with another private enterprise organization.
At the present time the provincial Government is offering to make a deal to carry out the exploration on the properties presently under the supervision of Sherritt Gordon, just as the provincial Government is doing the majority of the exploration in the area around Lynn Lake that is not directly under the control of the company. The company is sitting on the best leases, not because of any fault of its own, Mr. Speaker, but because at the present time it cannot afford to undertake the exploration, and because the federal Government's tax breaks, write-offs, depreciation and all the rest are so good that it does not want to give them up at the present time.
What 1 would ask of the federal Government is to do one of two things. It should make the Province eligible for a similar type of tax credit on the investment it puts into that area, therefore encouraging exploration at this time. As I stated earlier, the Province is willing to do this. It is only by exploration at this time that jobs in the Lynn Lake area will be saved. If that is not acceptable to the Government, then 1 would ask the Government to review its present tax write-off schemes for exploration, realizing that in this particular case those provisions are actually preventing exploration and may cause the death of a town, the loss of its businesses and the loss of the homes of the residents of that community.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: MINES AND MINING-CLOSING OF SHERRITT GORDON MINE AT LYNN LAKE, MAN. (B) REQUEST THAT TAX WRITE-OFF PROVISIONS BE CHANGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very
carefully to the concerns raised by the Hon. Member, in particular his last two or three sentences in which he requested that certain tax write-off provisions be changed. I have certain information before me, Mr. Speaker, I would like to share with the Hon. Member. Perhaps I could read information into the record and, if he believes it to be incorrect, perhaps we could discuss the matter further.
I am of the view that senior officials of Energy, Mines and Resources have checked with a senior official of Sherritt Gordon Mines Limited as to why the company would not accept money from the Province of Manitoba because of the federal Government's tax write-off procedures. The senior officials stated that no money has been offered to the company by the Manitoba Government. He also stated that an application by Sherritt Gordon for a grant under the NEED Program for further exploration of a gold deposit near Lynn Lake is being considered by the Manitoba and federal Governments and that taxation policies of the federal Government have not at any time entered into this matter.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, the provisions of the federal Income Tax Act have always provided considerable stimulation with respect to mining exploration. In addition, most of the Provinces follow the lead of the Government of Canada in this regard. For example, for several years now exploration expenditures have been deductible from any income, to the extent of that income. Since late 1978, mining exploration expenditures have included pre-production mine development expenditures, also deductible from any income.
In the budget of April 19 an additional measure was provided to stimulate mine exploration. As may be known, mining exploration earns depletion at a rate of $1 of depletion for each $3 of expenditure. Prior to the budget the earned depletion could only be deducted from resource income. This made it difficult at times for various interests participating in mining exploration ventures to claim the benefit. This was especially true for individuals and non-resource companies. The budget provided that the depletion earned after April 19 on exploration costs can also be deducted from any income for federal income tax purposes. As most of the Provinces will also recognize this incentive, the after-tax cost of the high risk mining exploration activity is significantly lowered for investors.
In view of the Government's recent commitment to further encourage mining exploration, it would not seem likely to me that the tax incentives for exploration would detract from the Sherritt Gordon application under the NEED grant, as the Hon. Member mentioned.
